Mapping the Phase Diagram of a Frustrated Magnet:
Flat Bands and Diabolical Locus from Irrep Collisions on the Pyrochlore Lattice

Kristian Tyn Kai Chung Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, Nöthnitzer Strasse 38, 01187 Dresden, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We map the complete classical phase diagram of the spin Hamiltonian describing pyrochlore rare-earth magnets with all symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbor bond-dependent anisotropic two-spin interactions. We provide a simple derivation of the organization of spins into tensor degrees of freedom describing the multipole moments of a tetrahedron, whose components correspond to irreducible representations (irreps) of the tetrahedral symmetry group TdT_{d}. By parameterizing the Hamiltonian directly in terms of the energies of the individual irreps, we perform an exhaustive search of all possible irrep degeneracies (collisions) which may host stable classical spin liquids arising at classical multi-critical points. We find four one-parameter families of models along which three phases are degenerate, all four of which merge at the Heisenberg antiferromagnetic point and its dual, and we give a complete three-dimensional picture of the phase diagram showing all of the phases and their intersections. The appearance of two copies of a single irrep implies an extra degenerate locus which pierces the phase boundaries at special points, yielding two additional isolated triple points. We demonstrate that one-parameter families of Hamiltonians are characterized by a topological invariant describing how the ground state spin configuration winds when adiabatically transported around this degenerate locus, analogous to a diabolical locus in quantum field theory. We provide a comprehensive catalog of all flat band degeneracies in the phase diagram and discuss the mechanisms that may allow for or impede the realization of a variety of classical spin liquids described by tensor gauge fields exhibiting nodal line singularities and concomitant multi-fold pinch points. Lastly, we provide a list of all cases where three irreps are degenerate above the ground state, which may lead to interesting features in the spin wave spectrum within each ordered phase.

I Introduction

The experimental search for, and theoretical classification of, exotic states of matter such as topological phases and deconfined critical points, along with their associated spectra of fractionalized excitations, is a central aim of modern condensed matter physics. A core focus is to understand systems whose low-energy physics is not characterized by conventional symmetry breaking with a “rigid” order parameter, but instead exhibits emergent liquid-like characteristics due to strong correlations. A central theme in this effort is that novel physics emerges when multiple conventional ordering channels compete with each other, becoming “intertwined” and resulting in physics that is more than the sum of individual parts Senthil et al. 2004a; Senthil et al. 2004b; Hermele et al. 2005; Balents et al. 2005; Senthil and Fisher 2006; Wang et al. 2017; Song et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2019; Zou et al. 2021. One class of systems that have made significant advancements through constant exchange between the experimental and theoretical fronts are frustrated magnets Lacroix et al. 2011; Diep 2020—specifically, magnetic insulators with antiferromagnetic spin interactions frustrated by triangular motifs, such as occurs on the triangular, kagome, and pyrochlore lattices. The geometric origin of the frustration makes such lattices highly favorable for supporting spin liquids—strongly correlated paramagnetic states which exhibit emergent deconfined gauge fields Balents 2010; Lhuillier and Misguich 2011; Savary and Balents 2016; Zhou et al. 2017; Wen et al. 2019; Knolle and Moessner 2019; Broholm et al. 2020.

In three spatial dimensions the pyrochlore lattice is the premier platform for frustrated magnetism, with multiple families of compounds for experimental study Subramanian et al. 1983; Gardner et al. 2010; Lee et al. 2010; Wiebe and Hallas 2015; Ghosh et al. 2019; Reig-i-Plessis and Hallas 2021 and a solid theoretical understanding of the microscopic physics Rau and Gingras 2019. It hosts two of the most well-known and canonical examples of spin liquids: the pyrochlore Heisenberg anti-ferromagnet (HAFM) Moessner and Chalker 1998; Henley 2005; Henley 2010 and the pyrochlore Ising anti-ferromagnet, more commonly known as spin ice Udagawa and Jaubert 2021; Castelnovo et al. 2012. Both of these are known to be classical spin liquids, which in the former case refers to the large-spin limit and in the latter refers to the limit where transverse spin-flipping terms are not included in the Hamiltonian.11 1 The latter is especially important because it is one of the only examples where we can derive perturbatively the quantum corrections and map them to a lattice gauge theory owing to the special geometry of the pyrochlore lattice Hermele et al. 2004; Benton et al. 2012; Savary and Balents 2012; Gingras and McClarty 2014, thus demonstrating the emergent gauge fields at the level of the microscopic spin operators, rather than as fluctuations about a mean field ground state Wen 2002. The number of references is far too great to list, see Ref. Udagawa and Jaubert 2021 for an overview and Refs. Smith et al. 2022; Porée et al. 2025; Gao et al. 2025; Smith et al. 2025 for more recent promising results for the realization of quantum spin ice in Cerium-based pyrochlores. These two models correspond to two distinct limiting cases of the symmetry-allowed spin Hamiltonian: completely isotropic interactions versus the maximally anisotropic limit where spins are constrained to point along their local high-symmetry easy-axes.

Over time the broader problem of considering all symmetry-allowed, bond-dependent, anisotropic spin interactions has become necessary as a plethora of pyrochlore materials have been synthesized and intensively studied Gardner et al. 2010. Spatial anisotropies are generically present in these magnets because the “spins” are actually crystal field doublets of f4\!f rare earth ions Bertin et al. 2012, for which strong spin-orbit coupling makes the interactions sensitive to the local crystalline symmetries Rau and Gingras 2019. Such bond-dependent anisotropies intermediate between the isotropic and easy-axis limits result in new types of frustration which can yield interesting novel spin liquids Rau et al. 2016; Essafi et al. 2017a; Maksimov et al. 2019, most famously in the exactly solved Kitaev Honeycomb model Kitaev 2006; Hermanns et al. 2018; Takagi et al. 2019. Indeed, within the phase diagram of the microscopic pyrochlore pseudo-spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with four symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbor spin couplings, a number of classical spin liquids beyond the HAFM and spin ice models have been discovered Taillefumier et al. 2017; Francini et al. 2025a; Benton et al. 2016; Yan et al. 2020; Lozano-Gómez et al. 2024a, including some exhibiting emergent tensor gauge fields Benton et al. 2016; Yan et al. 2020; Lozano-Gómez et al. 2024a, which are expected to describe fractonic spin liquids Pretko 2017a; Prem et al. 2018.

Despite many studies, however, a comprehensive picture of the entire phase diagram and how the various models studied fit together has not yet appeared. Given the maturity of research on pyrochlore magnetism, recent advances in the understanding of classical spin liquids Benton and Moessner 2021; Yan et al. 2024a; Yan et al. 2024b; Fang et al. 2024, along with many new avenues for experimental research Ghosh et al. 2019; Reig-i-Plessis and Hallas 2021; Nutakki et al. 2023, it is warranted to give a complete account of the phase diagram and the various places in it where spin liquidity exists or may be present, how the variety of known examples fit together, and how the tensorial nature of these spin liquids arises. Whereas previous studies have looked at either two-dimensional cross sections of the phase diagram Wong et al. 2013; Javanparast et al. 2015a; Yan et al. 2017; Rau and Gingras 2019; Wei and Curnoe 2023 or certain 1-parameter models Taillefumier et al. 2017; Noculak et al. 2023; Yan et al. 2020, it is highly desirable to have a complete picture that plainly visualizes how such cuts of the phase diagram fit together, along with how the variety of spin liquids coincide with special degeneracies of the phase diagram. Additionally, recent work in the study of so-called ‘diabolical loci” Hsin et al. 2020 and “unnecessary critical points” Bi and Senthil 2019; Jian and Xu 2020; Prakash et al. 2023; Prakash and Jones 2025 has emphasized that phase diagrams may contain non-trivial structures other than phase boundaries, and it would be interesting to know whether such structures exist in the phase diagrams of frustrated magnets. These are the tasks we take up in this paper.

A summary of the layout and core results are as follows. In Section II we introduce the Hamiltonian and its various parameterizations, where Fig. 1 illustrates the bond-dependent nature of the anisotropic interactions. We then explain the origin of the tensorial nature of pyrochlore spin liquids by deriving the tensor multipole decomposition of a single tetrahedron (Table 1) and exposing how it corresponds to an analysis of the irreducible representations (irreps) of the tetrahedral symmetry group, where each of the four distinct irreps corresponds to one ground state phase illustrated in Fig. 3. We pay particular attention to the “canting” of spins due to the continuous mixing of two copies of the T1T_{1} irrep appearing in the symmetry decomposition, illustrated in Fig. 4. In Section IV we then take up the issue of parameterizing the Hamiltonian in a way that can be used to expose all of the possible ground state degeneracies, which we accomplish by inverting the relation between the irrep energies and the exchange parameters, which allows the irrep energies to be tuned independently. This enables us to give the complete classification of all of the multi-critical loci where ground state irreps collide, i.e. different phases become degenerate and thus compete and potentially intertwine to produce spin liquids, as evidenced by the presence of flat bands in the interaction matrix. In particular, we show that there is one point in the phase diagram where all four phases become degenerate—the maximally symmetric HAFM. It lies at the meeting point of four triple lines, listed in Table 3. We provide a complete picture of the full phase diagram in Footnote 13, which shows all of the phases, phase boundaries, and the four triple lines which merge at the HAFM point. In the process we uncover a locus along which the two copies of the repeated T1T_{1} irrep are degenerate, and in Section V we show that this special locus defines a topological invariant for 1-parameter families of models which encircle it, analogous to a diabolical locus or conical intersection. Finally, in Section VI we give a full catalog of all degenerate combinations which yield flat band degeneracies in Tables 6, 6 and 6, along with the spin structure factors computed in the self-consistent Gaussian approximation in Figs. 10 and 11, and discuss the connection between pinch lines and fourfold pinch points in tensor spin liquids, illustrated in Fig. 13. We end in Section VII with a discussion of all triple degeneracies that occur in excited states, shown in Fig. 14, which give the phase diagram some further interesting structure and may have interesting imprints on the excitations above the ground state within each phase.

II Symmetry Classification of Ground States

For rare earth pyrochlore magnetic insulators with the familiar R2​M2​O7\text{R}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{M}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{7}}} structure, the magnetic ff-electron rare earth (R) ions form a pyrochlore lattice of corner-sharing tetrahedra, shown in Fig. 1(a), with the transition metal (M) ions forming a second interwoven pyrochlore lattice (not shown) Rau and Gingras 2019; Subramanian et al. 1983; Gardner et al. 2010. Each rare earth ion sits in the center of a distorted cube of oxygen atoms shown in Fig. 1(b), which generate local crystal fields that split the electronic ground state degeneracy of the central ion. In most such compounds this results in a crystal field ground state doublet typically protected by a gap of order 100100K Bertin et al. 2012, and the full crystal field Hamiltonian can be projected into this doublet Hilbert space to obtain an effective low-energy pseudo-spin-1/2 Hamiltonian. There are three allowed types of doublets—Kramers effective-spin-1/2; Kramers dipolar-octupolar; and non-Kramers Rau and Gingras 2018; Rau and Gingras 2019. For the effective spin-1/2 doublet the pseudo-spin operators transform as ordinary dipoles, and its most general Hamiltonian is our main concern in this work. For the non-Kramers doublet the local-zz operators transform as dipoles while the local-x​yxy operators transform as quadrupoles, so they cannot couple, but its Hamiltonian is just a restricted version of that of the effective spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with one coupling set to zero. The dipolar-octupolar case has a different Hamiltonian which reduces to a simple XYZ-model, and we will not consider it here.22 2 The dipolar-octupolar classical phase diagram can be parameterized as the surface of a cube, with three copies of the spin ice phase and three copies of the all-in-all-out phase on the six faces Huang et al. 2014.

We consider the most general nearest-neighbor spin model on the pyrochlore lattice,

H=12​∑i,j∑α,β∈{x,y,z}Siα​𝒥i​jα​β​Sjβ,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\{x,y,z\}}S_{i}^{\alpha}\mathcal{J}_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}S_{j}^{\beta}, (1a)

where the first sum is over sites ii and jj of the pyrochlore lattice and α,β\alpha,\beta index the three components of a spin. The matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J} contains all symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbor spin-spin interactions, and we refer to it as the interaction matrix, restricting to only nearest-neighbor interactions. The allowed couplings can be deduced by symmetry by considering all spatial symmetries which swap two spins at sites ii and jj, and demanding that ∑α​βSiα​𝒥i​jα​β​Sjβ\sum_{\alpha\beta}S_{i}^{\alpha}\mathcal{J}_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}S_{j}^{\beta} be invariant.

II.1 Parameterizations of Anisotropic Interactions

The Hamiltonian can be parameterized either in a global or a local basis, each of which can be useful to identify special parameter points Yan et al. 2017; Rau and Gingras 2019; Ross et al. 2011. If we take α,β\alpha,\beta in Eq. 1a to refer to the global frame Cartesian components of a spin, with xx, yy, and zz axes along the cubic symmetry axes, then for two spins in the x,yx,y plane the interaction matrix has four independent components,

𝒥i​jα​β=(J1J3−J4J3J1−J4J4J4J2)α​β.\mathcal{J}_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}[c]J_{1}&J_{3}&-J_{4}\\ J_{3}&J_{1}&-J_{4}\\ J_{4}&J_{4}&J_{2}\end{pmatrix}^{\alpha\beta}. (1b)

Since every nearest-neighbor bond is symmetry-equivalent, there are four free parameters in the Hamiltonian.

These symmetry-allowed interactions can equivalently be parameterized in a coordinate-free notation as (T\mathrm{T} denotes transpose)

H=∑⟨i​j⟩\displaystyle H=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} [JHeis𝑺i⋅𝑺j+JPD𝑺i[𝒓^i​j𝒓^i​jT]𝑺j+JK𝑺i[𝒏^i​j𝒏^i​jT]𝑺j\displaystyle\Big[J_{\text{Heis}}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}+J_{\text{PD}}\bm{S}_{i}[\hat{\bm{r}}_{ij}\hat{\bm{r}}_{ij}^{\mathrm{T}}]\bm{S}_{j}+J_{\text{K}}\bm{S}_{i}[\hat{\bm{n}}_{ij}\hat{\bm{n}}_{ij}^{\mathrm{T}}]\bm{S}_{j}
+JDM𝑫i​j⋅(𝑺i×𝑺j)]+JSIA2∑i|𝑺i⋅𝒛^i|2,\displaystyle+J_{\text{DM}}\bm{D}_{ij}\cdot(\bm{S}_{i}\times\bm{S}_{j})\Big]+\frac{J_{\text{SIA}}}{2}\sum_{i}|\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\hat{\bm{z}}_{i}|^{2}, (2)

where we refer to the four interactions as: isotropic Heisenberg (Heis), pseudo-dipolar (PD), Kitaev-like (K), Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM), and we also include a single-ion anisotropy (SIA).33 3 While single-ion anisotropy is irrelevant for spin-1/2 operators, it will be important for us to include since it is a symmetry-allowed parameter required to match the number of parameters in the Hamiltonian with the number of irreducible representations of the point symmetry group, thus allowing us to invert the relation between irrep energies and exchange parameters in Section III. The geometry of these bond-dependent anisotropic interactions is illustrated in Fig. 1, which shows a single tetrahedron of the pyrochlore lattice inscribed in a cube: 𝒓^i​j∝𝒓j−𝒓i\smash{\cramped{\hat{\bm{r}}_{ij}\propto\bm{r}_{j}-\bm{r}_{i}}} point from site ii to site jj (gray arrows), where 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} is the position of site ii; 𝒏^i​j\hat{\bm{n}}_{ij} are the normal vectors to the cube faces (orange arrows); and 𝑫^i​j=𝒏^i​j×𝒓^i​j\smash{\cramped{\hat{\bm{D}}_{ij}=\hat{\bm{n}}_{ij}\times\hat{\bm{r}}_{ij}}} are the DM vectors (blue arrows). We call the third term Kitaev-like because it involves only xx, yy, or zz spin interactions on each edge—a zz-zz interaction if 𝒓i​j\bm{r}_{ij} is in the x,yx,y plane and the others by cyclic permutation. The pseudo-dipolar term is so called because it appears when truncating a dipole-dipole interaction at nearest-neighbor. In the single-ion anisotropy, 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} is the local easy-axis direction.

In addition to the global frame, one can utilize a local symmetry-adapted basis, with a separate frame defined for each spin. The standard definitions take the local 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} along the 3-fold easy-axis, 𝒚^i\hat{\bm{y}}_{i} along a 2-fold axis, and 𝒙^i=𝒚^i×𝒛^i\hat{\bm{x}}_{i}=\hat{\bm{y}}_{i}\times\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} lying in a mirror plane. An explicit choice of local coordinates is given in Appendix A. The relations between the three parameterizations Eq. 1b, Eq. 2, and Eq. 3 are given in Appendix C. The local basis parameters in Eq. 3 will play a key role throughout this work, as they expose a number of important symmetries and dualities. In particular, the Hamiltonian has a duality by applying a π\pi rotation to each spin about its local 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} axis and changing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}. Furthermore, when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, there is an additional duality applying a π/2\pi/2 rotation to each spin about its local axis and switching the sign of J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm}.

In this work we will set JSIA=0\cramped{J_{\text{SIA}}=0}, as is appropriate for effective spin-1/2 systems where (Siz)2(S_{i}^{z})^{2} is a constant multiple of the identity. However, for the purpose of the symmetry irreducible representation analysis we will employ, however, it is important that we keep JSIAJ_{\text{SIA}} as a formal parameter. The symmetry analysis does not know about the underlying spin quantum number, only the vector transformation properties of the spin operators. Since= single ion anisotropy us a symmetry-allowed coupling, its inclusion matches the number of parameters in the Hamiltonian with the number of tunable eigenvalues of the interaction matrix. This matching is necessary to invert their relation and re-parameterize the phase diagram in terms of the eigenvalues, which is key to our mapping of the phase diagram. One can consider turning on single-ion anisotropy adiabatically starting from the phase diagram we present here, which will drive the system towards either the easy-plane or easy-axis configurations.

In this work we will treat the spins as classical fixed-length vectors, with spin length normalized to unity, |𝑺i|2=1|\bm{S}_{i}|^{2}=1. There are two ways to justify this classical approximation. The standard view is that it arises in the large-SS limit of the quantum model. An alternative perspective is that it is the restriction of the quantum S=1/2S=1/2 problem to the variational manifold of unentangled product states, whose local degrees of freedom are SU(2) spin coherent states on the Bloch sphere, ℂ​P1≃S2\mathbbm{C}P^{1}\simeq S^{2}. While these two perspectives give the same interpretation—unentangled local dipole moments—the latter can be generalized to different spin quantum number. In particular, the approach can be modified to higher spin quantum number to account for multipolar degrees of freedom using SU(2​S+12S+1) coherent states Remund et al. 2022; Zhang and Batista 2021; Chung et al. 2025, particularly relevant in the case of spin-1 pyrochlores Zhang et al. 2019; Plumb et al. 2019; Hagymási et al. 2024.

II.2 Band Structure and Degeneracies

The classical phase diagram of this Hamiltonian can be mapped out by studying a single tetrahedron, because the Hamiltonian decomposes into identical copies on each tetrahedron tt,

H=12​∑t∑μ,ν=14∑α,βSt,μα​𝒥μ​να​β​St,νβ,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t}\sum_{\mu,\nu=1}^{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}S_{t,\mu}^{\alpha}\mathcal{J}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}S_{t,\nu}^{\beta}, (5)

where 𝑺t,μ\bm{S}_{t,\mu} is the spin on tetrahedron tt and sublattice μ\mu. The interaction matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J} is the same on every tetrahedron, and the factor of 1/2 accounts for the double-counting of each nearest-neighbor pair in the sum over μ\mu and ν\nu. Since the Hamiltonian is the same on every tetrahedron, by studying the ground states of a single tetrahedron the ground states of the entire system can be determined by “lego-brick-rules”, i.e. by attaching tetrahedra together at their corners and matching the corresponding spin Yan et al. 2017.

Another way to say this is to note that each FCC primitive unit cell contains four spins, and the possible uniform ground states, i.e. those that repeat in every FCC unit cell, must have the same spin configuration on every tetrahedron. Thus by solving the single-tetrahedron ground states, one can construct all the zero-wavevector ground states for the entire lattice. Because all of the interactions are internal to each tetrahedron, it follows that every single-tetrahedron ground state gives a uniform ground state for the entire system.

This can also be understood by diagonalizing the quadratic form in Eq. 1a via Fourier transform. Since 𝒥\mathcal{J} commutes with the magnetic space group symmetries, it is translationally invariant and thus block-diagonalized into 12×1212\times 12 blocks in the Fourier basis (corresponding to four 3-component spins per unit cell), each block labeled by a crystal momentum wavevector 𝒒\bm{q}. Diagonalizing therefore yields twelve bands of eigenvalues in reciprocal space, Jn​(𝒒)J_{n}(\bm{q}), where n=1,⋯12n=1,\cdots 12, each corresponding to a normalized eigenvector ψ𝒒,n\smash{\psi_{\bm{q},n}} and a corresponding normal mode

S𝒒,n=∑i∑α[ψ𝒒,n]iα​Siα,S_{\bm{q},n}=\sum_{i}\sum_{\alpha}[\psi_{\bm{q},n}]_{i}^{\alpha}S_{i}^{\alpha}, (6)

so that the Hamiltonian is diagonalized into a sum of decoupled quadratic modes

H=12​∑𝒒∑n=112Jn​(𝒒)​|S𝒒,n|2.H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{q}}\sum_{n=1}^{12}J_{n}(\bm{q})|S_{\bm{q},n}|^{2}. (7)

In principle, the minimum eigenvalue normal mode determines the ground state Luttinger and Tisza 1946; Litvin 1974.44 4 It may occur that one cannot use the corresponding eigenvectors to construct a state satisfying the spin-length constraint |𝑺i|2=1|\bm{S}_{i}|^{2}=1 on every site, in which case the ground state will necessarily include contributions from some higher-energy normal modes. This does not occur in the pyrochlore model we are considering here. With only nearest-neighbor interactions on the pyrochlore lattice, the minimum eigenvalue of the interaction matrix is always found at the Brillouin zone center. This is a direct consequence of the corner-sharing tetrahedral geometry: minimizing the energy of each tetrahedron simultaneously minimizes the energy of the full lattice, leaving no energetic incentive for spatially modulated order. As a result, the nearest-neighbor model supports only 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 ordered phases (or disordered phases). By contrast, further-neighbor interactions introduce additional 𝒒\bm{q}-dependence into the interaction matrix, producing higher-harmonic modulations of the bands that can shift the minimum to finite wavevector and thereby stabilize 𝒒≠0\bm{q}\neq 0 order.

The 𝒒=𝟎\cramped{\bm{q}=\bm{0}} block of the interaction matrix commutes with a 12-dimensional representation of the tetrahedral symmetry group Td⊆O⁡(3)\cramped{T_{d}\subseteq O(3)}.55 5 In full generality one could consider how the entire system transforms under the full space group. Since we only consider nearest-neighbor interactions within a unit cell, we restrict our attention to the point group Oh\mathrm{O}_{h}, which is the symmetry of a single primitive unit cell containing two tetrahedra. Furthermore, since we do not consider inversion-breaking breathing anisotropy, we can restrict our attention to the inversion-even subgroup Td≃Oh/ℤ2T_{d}\simeq\mathrm{O}_{h}/\mathbbm{Z}_{2}, or equivalently to the inversion-even (gerade) irreps of Oh\mathrm{O}_{h}. This representation decomposes into a collection of irreducible representations (irreps), and the dimensions of the irreps appearing in the decomposition correspond to the degeneracies of the eigenvalues at 𝒒=𝟎\cramped{\bm{q}=\bm{0}}, i.e. the symmetry protects a set of band touchings at the zone center, which we discuss in detail in Section II.3. Classical spin liquids arise when there is at least one flat band at the bottom of the spectrum Yan et al. 2024a; Yan et al. 2024b; Davier et al. 2023; Henley 2005; Isakov et al. 2004, which will be discussed in detail in Section VI. This generally occurs when multiple ground state irreps collide, with more irreps giving more degeneracy and more potential flat bands.

This is illustrated in Fig. 2. There are five distinct eigenvalues of the interaction matrix at the Γ\Gamma point, each labeled by an irreducible representation (irrep) of the point group TdT_{d} and discussed in detail in Section II.3, the degeneracy of the bands at the zone center corresponding to the dimension of the corresponding irrep. Figure 2(a) shows the band structure at a generic point in the phase diagram, where all five eigenvalues are distinct, and a quadratic band minimum at 𝒒=𝟎\bm{q}=\bm{0} (the Γ\Gamma point). Correspondingly, the system exhibits a unique uniform ground state (up to symmetry). Figure 2(b) shows the band structure at a point on a phase boundary between two phases, where two different irreps are degenerate at zero energy. This results in a flat line of zero-energy eigenvalues along the (h​h​h)(hhh) high-symmetry line (Γ→L\Gamma\to L, marked in red). Figure 2(c) shows the band structure on a triple line where three phases are degenerate, with three degenerate zero-energy irreps, exhibiting completely flat bands throughout the entire Brillouin zone. Lastly, Fig. 2(d) shows the band structure at the maximally isotropic Heisenberg antiferromagnet point, where four eigenvalues are degenerate at zero energy. As we will show, at this special point all four phases meet, and the system exhibits the maximum zero-energy degeneracy, with six of twelve bands completely flat.

II.3 Irreducible Representations and Multipole Decomposition

While the irreducible representation analysis has been known and utilized to study the phase diagram Yan et al. 2017; Pandey et al. 2020, we present here an intuitive derivation that directly relates it to the multipole moments of a tetrahedron. Consider four spins on the corners of a single tetrahedron, with a total of twelve components SμαS_{\mu}^{\alpha}. Under the action of TdT_{d}, the corners of the tetrahedron are permuted while the spins rotate as angular momenta (i.e. pseudo-vectors). We thus have a 12-dimensional representation of TdT_{d}, where each g∈Tdg\in T_{d} is represented by a 12×1212\times 12 matrix ρ⁡(g)\rho(g), such that after a rotation the spin components are given by

[ρ⁡(g)​S]μα=∑ν,β[ρ⁡(g)]μ​να​β​Sνβ.[\rho(g)S]_{\mu}^{\alpha}=\sum_{\nu,\beta}[\rho(g)]_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}S_{\nu}^{\beta}. (8)

This is a tensor product representation of a four-dimensional permutation representation and a 3-dimensional pseudo-vector representation, i.e. it can be decomposed as

[ρ⁡(g)]μ​να​β=[π⁡(g)]μ​ν​[R¯​(g)]α​β,[\rho(g)]_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}=[\pi(g)]_{\mu\nu}[\bar{R}(g)]^{\alpha\beta}, (9)

where π⁡(g)\pi(g) is a permutation matrix and R¯​(g)\bar{R}(g) is a pseudo-vector rotation matrix, R¯​(g)≡det[R⁡(g)]​R​(g)\bar{R}(g)\equiv\det[R(g)]R(g) with R⁡(g)R(g) an ordinary rotation matrix.66 6 For example, a reflection acts on a polar vector as −1-1 (inversion) times a π\pi rotation in the reflection plane, while on a pseudovector (axial vector) it acts only as a π\pi rotation.

The fact that this is a tensor product representation allows us to straightforwardly deduce the structure of the irrep decomposition and construct the corresponding invariant linear combinations of spin components. First, we note that TdT_{d} has five irreducible representations, which are commonly denoted A1A_{1}, A2A_{2}, EE, T1T_{1}, and T2T_{2}, and which we also denote by 𝟏\bm{1}, 𝟏¯\bm{\bar{1}}, 𝟐\bm{2}, 𝟑¯\bm{\bar{3}}, and 𝟑\bm{3}, respectively. The number indicates the dimension of the irrep while the bar indicates that it picks up an additional sign under inversions—𝟏{\bm{1}} is a scalar representation, 𝟏¯\bar{\bm{1}} is a pseudoscalar representation, 𝟑{\bm{3}} is a vector representation, 𝟑¯\bar{\bm{3}} is a pseudovector representation. In particular, the T1T_{1} or 𝟑¯\bm{\bar{3}} irrep acts as pseudovector rotations, while the T2T_{2} or 𝟑\bm{3} irrep acts as vector rotations. Let 𝟏𝟐\bm{12} denote the full twelve-dimensional reducible representation ρ\rho, and let 𝟒\bm{4} denote the permutation representation, then starting from Eq. 9 we have

𝟏𝟐\displaystyle\bm{12} =𝟒⊗𝟑¯\displaystyle=\bm{4}\otimes\bm{\bar{3}}
=(𝟏⊕𝟑)⊗𝟑¯\displaystyle=(\bm{1}\oplus\bm{3})\otimes\bm{\bar{3}}
=(𝟏⊗𝟑¯)⊕(𝟑⊗𝟑¯).\displaystyle=(\bm{1}\otimes\bm{\bar{3}})\oplus(\bm{3}\otimes\bm{\bar{3}}). (10)

Here we have utilized a simple fact: every permutation representation always contains into a single copy of the trivial representation 𝟏\bm{1} plus a remainder. Furthermore, the permutation representation is faithful, so the remainder must be the faithful 𝟑\bm{3} irrep.77 7 Faithful means that no two group elements map to the same matrix in the representation. We can thus anticipate that the twelve dimensional representation can be decomposed into a 3-component pseudovector which is invariant under permuting the spins (𝟏⊗𝟑\bm{1}\otimes\bm{3}), and the remaining nine spin components can be grouped into a 3×33\times 3 tensor This tensor will naturally decompose into its scalar trace, its three anti-symmetric components, and its five symmetric components,88 8 The trace corresponds to the 𝟏¯\bm{\bar{1}} representation since one index of the tensor picks up an extra sign under inversions. Similarly, the anti-symmetric part of a rank-2 tensor would normally act as a pseudovector, but the extra sign turns it into a proper vector. We put the bar on the 𝟓¯\bm{\bar{5}} to indicate that this piece also gets the extra sign.

𝟏𝟐=𝟑¯⊕(𝟏¯⊕𝟑⊕𝟓¯),\bm{12}=\bm{\bar{3}}\oplus(\bm{\bar{1}}\oplus\bm{3}\oplus\bm{\bar{5}}), (11)

Since TdT_{d} only has irreps up to three dimensions, the 𝟓\bm{5} irrep must decompose further into 𝟐⊕𝟑¯\bm{2}\oplus\bar{\bm{3}} corresponding to the trace-free diagonal and symmetric off-diagonal tensor components. In sum, we have the final decomposition

𝟏𝟐\displaystyle\bm{12} =𝟑¯⊕(𝟏¯⊕𝟑⊕(𝟐⊕𝟑¯))\displaystyle=\bm{\bar{3}}\oplus(\bm{\bar{1}}\oplus\bm{3}\oplus(\bm{2}\oplus\bm{\bar{3}}))
≡T1∥⊕(A2⊕T2⊕(E⊕T1⟂)),\displaystyle\equiv\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\oplus(A_{2}\oplus T_{2}\oplus(E\oplus\smash{T_{1\perp}})), (12)

where we have given two distinct labels to the two copies of the T1T_{1} (𝟑¯\bar{\bm{3}}) irrep. Each of the irreps corresponds to a ground state of the tetrahedron. Each irrep II corresponds to a linear combination of the four spins with the general form

mIa=12​∑μ(𝝍^Ia)μ⋅𝑺μ,m_{I}^{a}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu}(\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{I}^{a})_{\mu}\cdot\bm{S}_{\mu}, (13)

where aa indexes the components of the irrep. Each corresponds to a distinct set of ground states of the tetrahedron where the spins are aligned along the local vectors (𝝍^Ia)μ(\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{I}^{a})_{\mu}, which are summarized in Table 1.

II.3.1 Multipole Decomposition

Here we give these irreps physical meaning as magnetic multipole moments of the tetrahedron. Thinking of the four spins as an array of dipoles, we construct the net dipole moment (rank-1) and the net rank-2 moment tensor as

𝒟α∝∑i∈tSiαℬα​β∝∑i∈triα​Siβ,\mathcal{D}^{\alpha}\propto\sum_{i\in t}S_{i}^{\alpha}\qquad\mathcal{B}^{\alpha\beta}\propto\sum_{i\in t}r_{i}^{\alpha}S_{i}^{\beta}, (14)

where 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} is the position of the ii’th spin relative to the center of the tetrahedron. These correspond to the 𝟑¯\bar{\bm{3}} and (𝟑⊗𝟑¯CLOSE(\bm{3}\otimes\bar{\bm{3}} terms in the decomposition. The rank-2 moment decomposes into its trace—the magnetic monopole moment (𝟏¯\bar{\bm{1}}); its antisymmetric part—the magnetic toroidal dipole moment (𝟑\bm{3}); and its symmetric trace-free part—-the magnetic quadrupole moment (𝟓¯\bar{\bm{5}}). For a system with full O⁡(3)O(3) symmetry, the 5-component quadrupole tensor would be irreducible, but when restricting to the subgroup of cubic symmetries it decomposes into 𝟓=𝟐⊕𝟑\cramped{\bm{5}=\bm{2}\oplus\bm{3}}.

𝑻𝟏∥\bm{T_{1\parallel}} Dipole Moment—The obvious normal mode is the net magnetic dipole moment of a single tetrahedron, which we normalize as

𝒟α≡mT1∥α=12∑μSμα=12∑μ𝒆^α⋅𝑺μ,\mathcal{D}^{\alpha}\equiv m_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu}S_{\mu}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu}\hat{\bm{e}}^{\alpha}\cdot\bm{S}_{\mu}, (15)

where we defined 𝒆^α\hat{\bm{e}}^{\alpha} as the unit vector pointing along the global Cartesian axis α∈{x,y,z}\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}. We use the symbol 𝒟\mathcal{D} to denote that this corresponds to the net moment of the tetrahedron. This quantity is invariant under permutations of the four sublattices, so corresponds to the factor (𝟏⊗𝟑¯)(\bm{1}\otimes\bm{\bar{3}}) in Eq. 10, or T1∥\smash{T_{1\parallel}} in Eq. 12. As a sum of spins it naturally transforms as a pseudovector. This normal mode is saturated when the four spins are collinear, corresponding to a set of ferromagnetic ground states shown in Fig. 3(e).

The remaining degrees of freedom are packaged into the rank-2 moment tensor transforming in the (𝟑⊗𝟑¯)(\bm{3}\otimes\bar{\bm{3}}) representation, which we normalize as

𝓑=32​∑μ𝒛^μ⊗𝑺μ,ℬα​β=32​∑μz^μα​Sμβ,\bm{\mathcal{B}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}\otimes\bm{S}_{\mu},\quad\mathcal{B}^{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\hat{z}_{\mu}^{\alpha}S_{\mu}^{\beta}, (16)

where we have replaced the displacement from the center of the tetrahedron 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} in Eq. 14 with their unit vector equivalents, which are the same as the four easy-axis unit vectors 𝒛^μ\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu} (red arrows in Fig. 1). The remaining normal modes are extracted by decomposing this tensor into its trace, anti-symmetric, and symmetric components.

𝑨𝟐\bm{A_{2}} Monopole Moment—The simplest irrep is the psuedo-scalar A2A_{2} irrep, extracted from the trace of ℬ\mathcal{B},99 9 Note that each 𝒎I\bm{m}_{I} is defined with a normalization factor so that Eq. 13 is satisfied, which ensures that each is a linear combinations of spins, ∑μ,αcμα​Sμα\sum_{\mu,\alpha}c_{\mu}^{\alpha}S_{\mu}^{\alpha}, where the coefficients cμαc_{\mu}^{\alpha} form a unit-length twelve-component vector.

3​mA2:=∑αℬα​α=32​∑μ𝒛^μ⋅𝑺μ.\sqrt{3}m_{A_{2}}:=\sum_{\alpha}\mathcal{B}^{\alpha\alpha}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}\cdot\bm{S}_{\mu}. (17)

This normal mode is saturated when the spins are “all-out” or “all-in” along their local easy-axes. Such an all-in-all-out configurations is shown in Fig. 3(a). This scalar changes sign under inversion since the spins transform as angular momenta, thus transforming as the A2A_{2} irrep. It is natural to identify as the magnetic monopole moment or “magnetic charge” of the spin configuration, and indeed it behaves as such in real materials Castelnovo et al. 2008.

𝑻𝟐\bm{T_{2}} Toroidal Dipole Moment—Next we can extract the anti-symmetric part,

2​mT2α:=∑β,γϵα​β​γ​ℬβ​γ=32​∑μ(𝒛^μ×𝒆^α)⋅𝑺μ.\sqrt{2}m_{T_{2}}^{\alpha}:=\sum_{\beta,\gamma}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma}\mathcal{B}^{\beta\gamma}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sum_{\mu}(\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}\times\hat{\bm{e}}^{\alpha})\cdot\bm{S}_{\mu}. (18)

First, note that this contains no contributions from the easy-axis components which are killed by the cross product, thus it corresponds to a set of ground states with spins orthogonal to their easy-axes. This normal mode is saturated when the spins are coplanar and form a chiral configuration relative to one of the Cartesian axes, known as the Palmer-Chalker ground states Palmer and Chalker 2000. There are six such ground states, corresponding to two chiralities about each of the three Cartesian cubic axes, one is shown in Fig. 3(d).

𝑻𝟏⟂\bm{T_{1\perp}} Quadrupole Moment (off-diagonal)---Lastly we have the symmetric part of the tensor, the five-component quadrupole moment, which separates under cubic symmetries into its diagonal-trace-free and off-diagonal parts.1010 10 This decomposition is widely known as eg⊕t2​ge_{g}\oplus t_{2g} in the context of the larger cubic point symmetry group OhO_{h}. The symmetric off-diagonal components of the tensor can be extracted by defining

2​mT1⟂α=∑β,γ|ϵα​γ​β|​ℬγ​β=32​∑μ∑β,γ|ϵα​γ​β|​z^μγ​Sμβ,\sqrt{2}m_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}^{\alpha}=\sum_{\beta,\gamma}|\epsilon^{\alpha\gamma\beta}|\mathcal{B}^{\gamma\beta}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sum_{\mu}\sum_{\beta,\gamma}|\epsilon^{\alpha\gamma\beta}|\hat{z}_{\mu}^{\gamma}S_{\mu}^{\beta}, (19)

the corresponding normal mode vectors lie in the Cartesian plane orthogonal to the α\alpha axis with two pointing towards the central axis and the other two pointing away, shown in Fig. 3(f). To see this, note that for each α\alpha the matrix PαP^{\alpha} with components Pβ​γα=|ϵα​β​γ|P_{\beta\gamma}^{\alpha}=|\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma}| acts as (i) a projector orthogonal to 𝒆^α\hat{\bm{e}}^{\alpha} and (ii) a reflection swapping the remaining two Cartesian axes. It projects each 𝒛^μ\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu} into one Cartesian plane, where they all point away from the center of the tetrahedron, then two of them on opposite corners are mirrored.

𝑬\bm{E} Quadrupole Moment (diagonal)—Finally, the diagonal-trace-free part. This is the hardest to represent in a simple geometric form, but it can be expressed as the three components of ℬα​α−(1/3)​Tr⁡ℬ\mathcal{B}^{\alpha\alpha}-(1/3)\Tr\mathcal{B}. By construction only two of the components are linearly independent since summing over α\alpha yields zero. However, there is a freedom to distribute the trace subtraction over the three elements. It is useful therefore to define a 3-component quantity which contains the diagonal components, combining the A2A_{2} and EE irreps together,

𝒬α=ℬα​α\mathcal{Q}^{\alpha}=\mathcal{B}^{\alpha\alpha} (20)

such that the trace is given by

𝒬A2≡3​mA2:=Tr⁡ℬ=(1,1,1)⋅𝓠.\mathcal{Q}_{A_{2}}\equiv\sqrt{3}\,m_{A_{2}}:=\Tr\mathcal{B}=(1,1,1)\cdot\bm{\mathcal{Q}}. (21)

We can then separate the trace-free EE components by choosing two basis vectors orthogonal to (1,1,1)(1,1,1), defining

𝒬ψ2≡3​mEψ2\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\psi_{2}}\equiv\sqrt{3}\,m_{E}^{\psi_{2}} =3​𝒙^1⋅𝓠​with​𝒙^1=16​(1,1,−2),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}\,\hat{\bm{x}}_{1}\cdot\bm{\mathcal{Q}}\,\,\,\text{with}\,\,\,\hat{\bm{x}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1,1,-2), (22a)
𝒬ψ3≡3​mEψ3\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\psi_{3}}\equiv\sqrt{3}\,m_{E}^{\psi_{3}} =3​𝒚^1⋅𝓠​with​𝒚^1=12​(1,−1,0),\displaystyle=\sqrt{3}\,\hat{\bm{y}}_{1}\cdot\bm{\mathcal{Q}}\,\,\,\text{with}\,\,\,\hat{\bm{y}}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,-1,0), (22b)

which are then packaged into the 2-component EE normal mode,

𝒎Ea=(mEψ2mEψ3)a.\bm{m}_{E}^{a}=\begin{pmatrix}m_{E}^{\psi_{2}}\\[4.0pt] m_{E}^{\psi_{3}}\end{pmatrix}^{a}. (23)

The corresponding ordering vectors are harder to write down than the previous ones, but they can be obtained by noting that 𝒙^1\hat{\bm{x}}_{1} and 𝒚^1\hat{\bm{y}}_{1} form an orthonormal basis with 𝒛^1\hat{\bm{z}}_{1} on one corner of the tetrahedron, which can be extended to an orthonormal basis {𝒙^μ,𝒚^μ,𝒛^μ}\{\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mu},\hat{\bm{y}}_{\mu},\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}\} on each of the four corners of the tetrahedron using the fourfold improper rotation symmetry (ninety degree rotations about a Cartesian axis followed by mirroring through the orthogonal plane), given explicitly in Appendix A. These correspond to the so-called ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} configurations, shown in Fig. 3(b,c), where in the ψ2\psi_{2} configurations spins lie in local mirror planes, while in the ψ3\psi_{3} configurations spins lie along a local 2-fold rotation axis.

II.3.2 Single Tetrahedron Irrep Energies

Inverting these definitions, we can re-package the irrep normal modes mIam_{I}^{a} into the vector and tensor degrees of freedom as

𝓓\displaystyle\bm{\mathcal{D}} =(mT1∥xmT1∥ymT1∥z),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}m_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}^{x}\\[1.0pt] m_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}^{y}\\[1.0pt] m_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}^{z}\end{pmatrix}, (24a)

(24c)

Thus we have demonstrated how the irreducible representation normal modes can be conveniently packaged into a tensors which encode the tetrahedral multipole moments. We can compute the energies of the different irreps, i.e. the 𝒒=𝟎\bm{q}=\bm{0} eigenvalues in Eq. 7, as1111 11 The prefactor normalizes the (𝝍^Ia)μ(\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{I}^{a})_{\mu} when treated as a single 12-component vector. Note that since these are defined as unit vectors on each sublattice, it follows that ∑μ|(𝝍^Ia)μ|2=2\sum_{\mu}|(\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{I}^{a})_{\mu}|^{2}=2.

JIa=14​∑μ>ν∑α​β(ψ^Ia)μα​𝒥μ​να​β​(ψ^Ia)νβ.J_{I}^{a}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\mu>\nu}\sum_{\alpha\beta}(\hat{\psi}_{I}^{a})_{\mu}^{\alpha}\mathcal{J}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\hat{\psi}_{I}^{a})_{\nu}^{\beta}. (25)

For I≠T1I\neq T_{1}, these are the components of the 𝒒=𝟎\bm{q}=\bm{0} eigenvectors of 𝒥\mathcal{J} on a single tetrahedron, and the JIaJ_{I}^{a} are the corresponding eigenvalues. Symmetry guarantees that eigenvalues corresponding to the same irrep II are degenerate, i.e. the JIa≡JI\smash{J_{I}^{a}\equiv J_{I}} are independent of aa. These values are listed in Table 2. The single-tetrahedron Hamiltonian can be expressed as

H=∑I∈{A2,E,T2,T1∥,T1⟂}JI|𝒎I|2+  2JT1∥⋅T1⟂𝒎T1∥⋅𝒎T1⟂H=\sum_{I\in\{A_{2},E,T_{2},\smash{T_{1\parallel}},\smash{T_{1\perp}}\}}J_{I}|\bm{m}_{I}|^{2}\,+\,\,2J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}\cdot\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}} (26)

|𝓓|2\displaystyle|\bm{\mathcal{D}}|^{2} =|𝒎T1∥|2\displaystyle=|\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}|^{2} (27a)

Tr⁡[𝓑​𝓑T]+|𝓓|2=∑I|𝒎I|2=∑μ|𝑺μ|2=const.\Tr[\bm{\mathcal{B}}\bm{\mathcal{B}}^{T}]+|\bm{\mathcal{D}}|^{2}=\sum_{I}|\bm{m}_{I}|^{2}=\sum_{\mu}|\bm{S}_{\mu}|^{2}=\text{const}. (28)

𝒎T1∥⋅𝒎T1⟂=12∑α​β​γ|ϵα​β​γ|𝒟αℬβ​γ.\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}\cdot\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{\alpha\beta\gamma}|\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma}|\mathcal{D}^{\alpha}\mathcal{B}^{\beta\gamma}. (29)

We discuss decoupling the two T1T_{1} irreps in the next section.

II.4 T1T_{1} Mixing and Canting Angle

Since there are two T1T_{1} irreps they can have a symmetry-allowed coupling in the Hamiltonian and can therefore mix. The T1∥\smash{T_{1\parallel}} and T1⟂\smash{T_{1\perp}} irrep order parameters derived from the multipole decomposition we will refer to as the global T1T_{1} irreps, since they involve the components of spins relative to the global Cartesian axes. Their coupling in the Hamiltonian is of the form

HT1∥⊕T1⟂=(𝒎T1∥𝒎T1⟂)T(JT1∥JT1∥⋅T1⟂JT1∥⋅T1⟂JT1⟂)(𝒎T1∥𝒎T1⟂),H_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\oplus\smash{T_{1\perp}}}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}\\ \bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\end{pmatrix}^{T}\begin{pmatrix}J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}&J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\\ J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}&J_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}\\ \bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\end{pmatrix}, (30)

where the cross term is controlled by the global J3J_{3} parameter in Eq. 1b and the single ion anisotropy,

JT1∥⋅T1⟂=23(JSIA+3J3),J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}(J_{\text{SIA}}+3J_{3}), (31)

which prefer for spins to cant away from the global Cartesian axes and towards the local three-fold axes. The amount of canting is determined by eliminating the coupling between the two T1T_{1} irreps, which is achieved by defining rotated T1T_{1} modes

(𝒎T1​ϕ𝒎T1​ϕ′)=(cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕ−sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ)​(𝒎T1∥𝒎T1⟂).\begin{pmatrix}\bm{m}_{T_{1\phi}}\\ \bm{m}_{T_{1\phi^{\prime}}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\phi&\sin\phi\\ -\sin\phi&\cos\phi\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}\\ \bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\end{pmatrix}. (32)

These rotated T1T_{1} modes have a simple interpretation: each spin cants in one of the mirror planes according to

mT1​ϕα=∑μ(cos⁡(ϕ)​𝒆^α+sin⁡(ϕ)​(𝝍^T1,⟂α)μ)⏟(𝝍^T1​ϕα)μ⋅𝑺μ.{m}^{\alpha}_{T_{1\phi}}=\sum_{\mu}\underbrace{(\cos(\phi)\hat{\bm{e}}^{\alpha}+\sin(\phi)(\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{T_{1,\perp}}^{\alpha})_{\mu})}_{(\displaystyle\hat{\bm{\psi}}_{T_{1\phi}}^{\alpha})_{\mu}}\cdot\bm{S}_{\mu}. (33)

and similarly for T1​ϕ′T_{1\phi^{\prime}}. The critical angle ϕc\phi_{c} for which the cross-term between the two T1T_{1} irreps vanishes is given in terms of the global irrep parameters by solving the equation

tan⁡(2​ϕc)=2JT1∥⋅T1⟂JT1⟂−JT1∥.\tan(2\phi_{c})=\frac{2J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}}{J_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}-J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}}. (34)

Note that ϕc\phi_{c} is only defined modulo π/2\pi/2, i.e. it does not tell us whether the T1T_{1} irrep with angle ϕc\phi_{c} or ϕc+π/2\phi_{c}+\pi/2 has lower energy. Diagonalizing the matrix in Eq. 30 yields the energies of the decoupled T1T_{1} normal modes

JT1±=12(JT1∥+JT1⟂±(JT1∥−JT1⟂)2+4JT1∥⋅T1⟂2),J_{T_{1\pm}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}+J_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}}\pm\sqrt{(J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}-J_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}})^{2}+4{J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}\cdot\smash{T_{1\perp}}}}^{2}}\,\right), (35)

where the ±\pm indicates the higher or lower energy eigenvalue. For solutions of Eq. 34 in the range ϕc∈(−π/4,π/4)\phi_{c}\in(-\pi/4,\pi/4), if JT1∥<JT1⟂J_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}<J_{\smash{T_{1\perp}}} then T1−=T1​ϕcT_{1-}=T_{1\phi_{c}}, while the opposite inequality implies T1−=T1​ϕc′T_{1-}=T_{1\phi_{c}^{\prime}}.

II.4.1 Easy-Axis Limit of T1T_{1} Irreps

It is through canting and mixing the two T1T_{1} irreps that one connects the global irreps to the local symmetry-adapted description in Eq. 3. Writing the canting angle equation Eq. 34 in terms of the local couplings,

tan⁡(2​ϕc)=2​2−72​Jz±2​J±+4​J±⁣±+Jz​z+16​2​Jz±−JSIA,\tan(2\phi_{c})=2\sqrt{2}-\frac{72J_{z\pm}}{2J_{\pm}+4J_{\pm\pm}+J_{zz}+16\sqrt{2}J_{z\pm}-J_{\text{SIA}}}, (36)

exposes a special critical angle—when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 the canting angle is given by

ϕ0≡tan−1⁡(2​2)/2=cos−1⁡(2/3).\phi_{0}\equiv\tan^{-1}(2\sqrt{2})/2=\cos^{-1}(\sqrt{2/3}). (37)

At this special canting angle, the local vectors in Eq. 33 are aligned along or orthogonal to the local three-fold axis 𝒛^μ\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}. This occurs precisely when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, i.e. when the local zz-components of the spin are completely decoupled from the local transverse components. We refer to the two corresponding irreps as

T1​ϕ0≡T1,planar,T1​ϕ0′≡T1,ice,T_{1\phi_{0}}\equiv T_{1,\text{planar}},\quad T_{1\phi_{0}^{\prime}}\equiv T_{1,\text{ice}}, (38)

using the notation of Ref. Yan et al. 2017. The T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} irrep corresponds to the ground states of spin ice, with two spins pointing “in” and two spins pointing “out” of the tetrahedron. The T1,planarT_{1,\text{planar}} irrep corresponds to ferromagnetic configurations with spins in their local easy-planes. It is very useful to express the canting angle relative to the [111][111] local easy-axes, rather than the [001][001] global Cartesian axes, by defining

θc=ϕc−ϕ0.\theta_{c}=\phi_{c}-\phi_{0}. (39)

From hereon we will refer to θc\theta_{c} as the canting angle, and ϕc\phi_{c} will not be used. Relative to the [111] axis, the analog of Eq. 34 is

tan⁡(2​θc)=2​JT1,ice⋅T1,planarJT1,ice−JT1,planar=8​Jz±2​J±+4​J±⁣±+Jz​z−JSIA.\tan(2\theta_{c})=\frac{2J_{T_{1,\text{ice}}\cdot T_{1,\text{planar}}}}{J_{T_{1,\text{ice}}}\!-J_{T_{1,\text{planar}}}}=\frac{8J_{z\pm}}{2J_{\pm}+4J_{\pm\pm}+J_{zz}-J_{\text{SIA}}}. (40)

The corresponding couplings are listed in Table 2. From this equation it is evident that switching the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} corresponds to switching the sign of θc\theta_{c}.

This is all summarized in Fig. 4, which shows how the spin configuration of the T1T_{1} irreps evolves as the canting angle rotates. To each configuration there is a corresponding dual configuration with the opposite sign of the canting angle, corresponding to a π\pi rotation of each spin about its local easy-axis. For a given set of exchange parameters, one of the two T1T_{1} irreps will have a lower energy; we denote the corresponding angle by θT1−\theta_{T_{1-}}, and the higher energy irrep has angle θT1+=θT1−+π/2\theta_{T_{1+}}=\theta_{T_{1-}}+\pi/2. These angles are defined modulo π\pi, since a π\pi rotation returns to the same T1T_{1} irrep with the spin directions reversed, i.e. the time-reversed state.

III Irrep Parameterization of the Model Space

In the remainder of this paper we will elucidate the structure of the full classical phase diagram of the nearest-neighbor spin-1/2 model on the pyrochlore lattice, focusing especially on the locations of the phase boundaries and the triple and quadruple points where three or four phases become degenerate, respectively. The irrep eigenvalues are given in Table 2. For a given set of parameters, the classical ground state is given by finding which irrep takes the minimum eigenvalue and aligning the spins along the associated ordering vectors in Eq. 13. For classical fixed-length vector spins this is the minimal energy state, and away from phase boundaries this should be an accurate product state ansatz for the quantum ground state. As we will see in detail, there are effectively four phases, one for each irrep if we don’t distinguish between the two T1T_{1} irreps. Each phase is the locus of parameter space within which one irrep has the lowest energy and the others are separated by a gap. In order to map the phase diagram it is crucial to identify the locus of parameters along which multiple ground states are degenerate, i.e. phase boundaries, triple points, and quadruple points.

III.1 Irrep Parameterization and Jz±J_{z\pm} Duality

Our strategy is to parameterize the phase diagram not in terms of the basis-dependent spin-spin couplings, but rather in terms of the basis-independent irrep energies JIJ_{I}. To achieve this, we first invert the relations in Table 2 in order to obtain the couplings as functions of the irrep eigenvalues. The resulting equations are

Jz​z\displaystyle J_{zz} =112​[3​JA2−2​JE−3​JT2−3​(JT1++JT1−)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{12}[3J_{A_{2}}-2J_{E}-3J_{T_{2}}-3(J_{T_{1+}}+J_{T_{1-}})] (41a)
J±\displaystyle J_{\pm} =−JE6\displaystyle=-\frac{J_{E}}{6} (41b)
J±⁣±\displaystyle J_{\pm\pm} =−112​(JE+3​JT2)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{12}(J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}) (41c)
|Jz±|\displaystyle|J_{z\pm}| =112​−(2​JE+3​JT2+3​JT1+)​(2​JE+3​JT2+3​JT1−)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{12}\sqrt{-(2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3J_{T_{1+}})(2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3J_{T_{1-}})} (41d)
JSIA\displaystyle J_{\text{SIA}} =14​[JA2+2​JE+3​JT2+3​(JT1−+JT1+)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}[J_{A_{2}}+2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3(J_{T_{1-}}+J_{T_{1+}})] (41e)

For any model with a given sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}, there is another model with the opposite sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} with the same irrep energies, because only its square appears in the irrep energies JT1±J_{T_{1\pm}} in Table 2.

This corresponds to a duality transformation of the Hamiltonian: applying a π\pi rotation of each spin about its local 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} axis sends Si±→−Si±S_{i}^{\pm}\to-S_{i}^{\pm}, changing the sign of the Sz​S±S^{z}S^{\pm} term in Eq. 3 while leaving the rest of the terms invariant. This sign change can then be cancelled by changing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}. Furthermore, such a rotation maps each irrep back to itself: A2A_{2} is clearly invariant under this transformation; for the easy-plane EE and T2T_{2} configurations this sends a spin configuration to its time-reversed configuration; and T1T_{1} configurations are turned into other T1T_{1} configurations. As such, reversing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} relates two Hamiltonians in the same phase. This is clear from Table 2 since the energies of the irreps are unchanged.

It is convenient to parameterize the splitting between the two T1T_{1} irreps,

JT1±≡JT1±Jδ​T1withJδ​T1≥0,J_{T_{1\pm}}\equiv J_{T_{1}}\pm J_{\delta T_{1}}\quad\text{with}\quad J_{\delta T_{1}}\geq 0, (42)

in order to write Eq. 41d in the form

|Jz±|=112​(3​Jδ​T1)2−(2​JE+3​JT2+3​JT1)2.|J_{z\pm}|=\frac{1}{12}\sqrt{(3J_{\delta T_{1}})^{2}-(2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3J_{T_{1}})^{2}}. (43)

In this form we can see the close relation between Jz±J_{z\pm} and the splitting of the two T1T_{1} irreps. In particular, there is a constraint on the possible eigenvalues,

3​Jδ​T1≥|2​JE+3​JT2+3​JT1|,3J_{\delta T_{1}}\geq|2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3J_{T_{1}}|, (44)

in order that Jz±J_{z\pm} is real. It is evident that if the two T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate (Jδ​T1=0J_{\delta T_{1}}=0) then Jz±J_{z\pm} must be zero, saturating the inequality. Equation 43 suggests that it is convenient to define a dimensionless parameter

α≡sign⁡(Jz±)​(2​JE+3​JT2+3​JT1)3​Jδ​T1,\alpha\equiv\sign(J_{z\pm})\frac{(2J_{E}+3J_{T_{2}}+3J_{T_{1}})}{3J_{\delta T_{1}}}, (45)

so that

|Jz±|=Jδ​T14​1−α2,|J_{z\pm}|=\frac{J_{\delta T_{1}}}{4}\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}, (46)

such that the inequality Eq. 44 is equivalent to |α|≤1|\alpha|\leq 1. The sign prefactor in Eq. 45 has been chosen because it allows us to interpret the canting formula Eq. 40 geometrically—it simplifies to

tan⁡(2​θc)=1−α2α=tan⁡(cos−1⁡(α)),\tan(2\theta_{c})=\frac{\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}}{\alpha}=\tan\left(\cos^{-1}(\alpha)\right), (47)

from which we obtain the convenient formula

θc=12​cos−1⁡(α)=cos−1⁡(α+12)modπ/2.\theta_{c}=\frac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}(\alpha)=\cos^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\alpha+1}{2}}\right)\mod\pi/2. (48)

III.2 Parameter Space vs. Model Space

Any real choice of the five symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbor spin-spin coupling parameters in Eq. 2 or Eq. 3, each a real number, defines an interaction matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J} and thus a Hamiltonian. We call this ℝ5\mathbbm{R}^{5} five-dimensional space the parameter space (ℝ4\mathbbm{R}^{4} if we set JSIA=0J_{\text{SIA}}=0). Within this space is a special point where all couplings are zero, corresponding to the trivial Hamiltonian H=0H=0. Many of the remaining non-trivial parameter sets are physically equivalent up to an overall energy scale. Ideally one would like to parameterize the space of Hamiltonians modulo such rescalings, which we call the model space.

One way to parameterize the model space is to simply take a unit sphere in the parameter space, e.g. using the local couplings in Eq. 3 (setting JSIA=0J_{\text{SIA}}=0)

Jz​z2+J±⁣±2+Jz±2+J±2=1.J_{zz}^{2}+J_{\pm\pm}^{2}+J_{z\pm}^{2}+J_{\pm}^{2}=1. (49)

Of course one could alternatively take the unit sphere in the basis J1⋯J4J_{1}\cdots J_{4} in Eq. 1a, or those in Eq. 2. The unit spheres in these spaces do not coincide, however, since the transformation relating these bases of the parameter space, Eqs. 4a and 4b, are not orthogonal. The parameter space does not have a canonical metric to measure distances between parameter sets or to define orthogonality, so such a choice of sphere is arbitrary. In any case such a choice does not yield a useful parameterization of the space of models. In this section we provide a parameterization by directly manipulating the irrep energies.

In full generality, a model is an equivalence class of parameters, where two parameter sets are equivalent if the band structure of the interaction matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J} eigenvalues (i.e. the Jn​(𝒒)J_{n}(\bm{q}) in Eq. 7) differ by either a shift or a re-scaling, i.e. a changing of the total bandwidth of the band structure of 𝒥\mathcal{J} without changing the band structure. For nearest-neighbor interactions the band structure of 𝒥\mathcal{J} is completely determined by the 𝒒=𝟎\bm{q}=\bm{0} eigenvalues, i.e. the irrep eigenvalues JIJ_{I}. Therefore, a set of irrep eigenvalues determines an interaction matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J}, with the caveats that (i) each allowed set of irrep eigenvalues corresponds to a pair of models with opposite signs of Jz±J_{z\pm}, and (ii) the inequality Eq. 44 must be satisfied for Jz±J_{z\pm} to be real. Consider then the 5-dimensional space of real irrep eigenvalues JIJ_{I}. We define an equivalence relation under affine rescalings

JI∼JI′ifJI′=a​JI+bJ_{I}\sim J_{I}^{\prime}\quad\text{if}\quad J_{I}^{\prime}=aJ_{I}+b (50)

for some real numbers aa and bb with a>0a>0. An equivalence class [JI][J_{I}] defines a model, and the space of equivalence classes is the model space, which has the topology of a 3-sphere.

III.3 Parameterizing the Model Space with JSIA=0J_{\text{SIA}}=0

In order to explore the model space, we require a parameterization which selects a single representative of each equivalence class of parameter sets, i.e. one which effectively fixes aa and bb in Eq. 50. To do so, we first choose an arbitrary energy scale J0J_{0} and measure each irrep energy relative to it, defining

JI=J0+ΔI.J_{I}=J_{0}+\Delta_{I}. (51)

To fix bb, we restrict the allowed parameter sets ΔI\Delta_{I} to those for which min⁡(ΔI)=0\mathrm{min}(\Delta_{I})=0. In other words, we fix the energy scale to be J0=min⁡(JI)J_{0}=\mathrm{min}(J_{I}), i.e. the ground state energy. In order to fix aa we have to fix the overall scale. Here many choices are possible, but the most obvious is to set max⁡(ΔI)=1\mathrm{max}(\Delta_{I})=1. In other words, we fix the total bandwidth of 𝒥\mathcal{J} to be unity, which is sensible because it is the natural energy scale in the Hamiltonian.

We note with this choice of scale, the L2L^{2} norm on the space of real eigenvalues induces a dimensionless metric on the model space, which can (in principle) be used to define how far apart two models are from each other. While the parameter space does not have a canonical metric, this would be the natural candidate for a “useful” metric—it measures how far apart two parameter sets are while holding the total bandwidth constant, i.e. modulo overall rescaling of the Hamiltonian. This may be a useful definition for quantitatively assessing how close a compound is to a phase boundary or a spin liquid Scheie et al. 2022.

For the purposes of this paper, we will set JSIA=0J_{\text{SIA}}=0, as is physically appropriate for spin-1/2 systems. This leads to helpful simplifications, but the analysis could be extended to include non-zero JSIAJ_{\text{SIA}}. Setting Eq. 41e equal to zero and solving for J0J_{0}, we obtain

J0=−112​[ΔA2+2​ΔE+3​ΔT2+3​(ΔT1−+ΔT1+)].J_{0}=-\frac{1}{12}\left[\Delta_{A_{2}}+2\Delta_{E}+3\Delta_{T_{2}}+3(\Delta_{T_{1-}}+\Delta_{T_{1+}})\right]. (52)

Substituting back into the remaining four equations, we obtain

Jz​z\displaystyle J_{zz} =136​[11​ΔA2−2​ΔE−3​ΔT2−3​(ΔT1−+ΔT1+)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{36}[11\Delta_{A_{2}}-2\Delta_{E}-3\Delta_{T_{2}}-3(\Delta_{T_{1-}}+\Delta_{T_{1+}})], (53a)
J±\displaystyle J_{\pm} =172​[ΔA2−10​ΔE+3​ΔT2+3​(ΔT1−+ΔT1+)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{72}[\Delta_{A_{2}}-10\Delta_{E}+3\Delta_{T_{2}}+3(\Delta_{T_{1-}}+\Delta_{T_{1+}})], (53b)
J±⁣±\displaystyle J_{\pm\pm} =136​(ΔA2−ΔE−6​ΔT2+3​(ΔT1−+ΔT1+)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{36}(\Delta_{A_{2}}-\Delta_{E}-6\Delta_{T_{2}}+3(\Delta_{T_{1-}}+\Delta_{T_{1+}})), (53c)
|Jz±|\displaystyle|J_{z\pm}| =136​(9​Δδ​T1)2−[2​ΔA2−2​ΔE−3​ΔT2+3​ΔT1]2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{36}\sqrt{(9\Delta_{\delta T_{1}})^{2}-[2\Delta_{A_{2}}-2\Delta_{E}-3\Delta_{T_{2}}+3\Delta_{T_{1}}]^{2}} (53d)

where in Eq. 53d we have defined for convenience the equivalent of Eq. 42, the average and the splitting between the two T1T_{1} irreps, ΔT1±=ΔT1±Δδ​T1\Delta_{T_{1\pm}}=\Delta_{T_{1}}\pm\Delta_{\delta T_{1}}, or inversely

ΔT1≡12​(ΔT1++ΔT1−),Δδ​T1≡12​(ΔT1+−ΔT1−)≥0.\Delta_{T_{1}}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_{T_{1+}}+\Delta_{T_{1-}}),\quad\Delta_{\delta T_{1}}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_{T_{1+}}-\Delta_{T_{1-}})\geq 0. (54)

The full model space is parameterized by tuning the ΔI\Delta_{I} subject to the constraints that

  1. 1.

    min⁡ΔI=0\min\Delta_{I}=0,

  2. 2.

    max⁡ΔI=1\max\Delta_{I}=1,

  3. 3.

    ΔT1+≥ΔT1−\Delta_{T_{1}+}\geq\Delta_{T_{1-}},

  4. 4.

    Jz±J_{z\pm} is real, i.e. Eq. 44 is satisfied.

The model space is 3-dimensional, since at a generic point with one ΔI\Delta_{I} set to zero and one set to unity there are three free parameters to vary. A phase is then the 3-dimensional locus of parameters where one of the ΔI\Delta_{I} is zero, and the rest are positive with the max fixed to unity. While there are five ΔI\Delta_{I} parameters, we will see there are only four distinct phases because the two T1T_{1} irreps mix continuously. Phase boundaries are two-dimensional and occur when two ΔI\Delta_{I} are zero while the remainder are positive. Triple points are one-dimensional lines along which three ΔI\Delta_{I} are zero, and the remaining one is allowed to vary. Lastly, it is possible to have a quadruple point, an isolated point where four phases are degenerate.

Note that while the model space has 0≤ΔI≤10\leq\Delta_{I}\leq 1, we will also allow the ΔI\Delta_{I} to vary outside this range in order to parameterize collections of models with interesting properties (i.e. irrep degeneracies) and to identify special points in the phase diagram (cf. Fig. 5). Such parameter sets can always be re-scaled uniquely back to the model space.

IV Mapping the Phase Diagram

The parameterization of Eq. 53 allows us to efficiently explore the parameter space in a way that makes the phase boundaries and special subspaces manifest, while decoupling the rescaling dimension. We will visualize the phase diagram by stereographically projecting the 3-sphere Eq. 49 into 3-dimensional space using the mapping

(Jz​z,J±⁣±,Jz±,J±)↦(X,Y,Z)≡(Jz​z1−J±,J±⁣±1−J±,Jz±1−J±).(J_{zz},J_{\pm\pm},J_{z\pm},J_{\pm})\mapsto(X,Y,Z)\equiv\left(\frac{J_{zz}}{1-J_{\pm}},\frac{J_{\pm\pm}}{1-J_{\pm}},\frac{J_{z\pm}}{1-J_{\pm}}\right). (55)

In particular, this 3-sphere has a 2-sphere subspace on which Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, dividing into into two hemispheres. Since the phases are dual under changing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}, the phase diagram in these two hemispheres is reflected through the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 “equator”, i.e. the “northern” and “southern” hemispheres of the phase diagram are mirror images of each other. For completeness, the inverse mapping of Eq. 55 is given by

(X,Y,Z)↦1R2+1​(2​X,2​Y,2​Z,R2−1),(X,Y,Z)\mapsto\frac{1}{R^{2}+1}\left(2X,2Y,2Z,R^{2}-1\right), (56)

where R2=X2+Y2+Z2R^{2}=X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}.

IV.1 Quadruple Points: Heisenberg Antiferromagnet

To map the structure of the phase diagram, we begin with the highest-degeneracy four-fold degenerate quadruple points. These can be searched for manually by setting all but one ΔI\Delta_{I} to zero in Eq. 53 and checking whether solutions exist with real Jz±J_{z\pm}. This immediately rules out the possibility of fourfold degeneracies with only A2A_{2}, EE, or T2T_{2} gapped. This leaves only one possibility: ΔT1+>0\Delta_{T_{1+}}>0 and all others are zero. This corresponds to the Heisenberg antiferromagnet (HAFM) point, with Hamiltonian

HHAFM=ΔT1+4∑⟨i​j⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j=E0+ΔT1+∑t|𝒎T1∥|2,H_{\text{HAFM}}=\frac{\Delta_{T_{1+}}}{4}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}=E_{0}+\Delta_{T_{1+}}\sum_{t}|\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}|^{2}, (57)

which has Jz±>0J_{z\pm}>0. The HAFM has a massively degenerate classical ground state manifold characterized by the zero-net-moment constraint 𝒎T1∥=𝟎\bm{m}_{\smash{T_{1\parallel}}}=\bm{0} on every tetrahedron, corresponding to the large degeneracy of the irreps. This is a prototypical example of a classical spin liquid, and has been extensively studied Reimers 1992; Canals and Lacroix 1998; Canals and Garanin 2001; Moessner and Chalker 1998; Isakov et al. 2004; Henley 2005; Henley 2010; Conlon and Chalker 2010; Iqbal et al. 2019. Since every model determined by a set of eigenvalues with Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0 has a dual with the opposite sign of Jz±J_{z\pm}, there is a second fourfold-degenerate point in the phase diagram which we will refer to as HAFMdual{}_{\text{dual}} Rau and Gingras 2019. The Hamiltonian at this point can be written as

HHAFMdual=E0+ΔT1+∑t|𝒎T1∥dual|2,H_{\text{HAFM${}_{\text{dual}}$}}=E_{0}+\Delta_{T_{1+}}\sum_{t}|\bm{m}_{T_{1\parallel}^{\text{dual}}}|^{2}, (58)

where the gapped T1∥dual\smash{T_{1\parallel}^{\text{dual}}} spin configuration, as well as the zero-energy T1⟂dual\smash{T_{1\perp}^{\text{dual}}}, are shown in Fig. 4.

IV.2 Triple Lines and Points

Starting from the HAFM points where all four phases are degenerate, ΔA2=ΔE=ΔT2=ΔT1−=0\Delta_{A_{2}}=\Delta_{E}=\Delta_{T_{2}}=\Delta_{T_{1-}}=0, one can lift the degeneracy of one of the four phases, thus tuning along a line where three phases are degenerate. The resulting parameter sets for these four triply degenerate lines are given in Table 3. For the ones where the gapped irrep is I′∈{A2,E,T2}I^{\prime}\in\{A_{2},E,T_{2}\}, the line can be parameterized by the ratio ΔI′/ΔT1+\Delta_{I^{\prime}}/\Delta_{T_{1+}}. The fourth line where both T1T_{1} irreps are gapped is better parameterized by the average and splitting of the two T1T_{1} irreps, Eq. 54.

The point ΔI′=0\Delta_{I^{\prime}}=0 corresponds to the two HAFM points, from which one can tune ΔI′/ΔT1+>0\Delta_{I^{\prime}}/\Delta_{T_{1+}}>0 continuously until it reaches a maximum allowed value at which Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0. Each line then continues by reversing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} and tuning ΔI′/ΔT1+\Delta_{I^{\prime}}/\Delta_{T_{1+}} back to zero, ending at the other HAFM point. Figure 5 shows the evolution of (a) the local exchange couplings, (b) the global exchange couplings, (c) the irrep energies, and (d) the canting angle along these lines. The right side of each plot with blue background is the region where the triply degenerate irreps are the ground state. The left side, with red background, has the triply degenerate irreps in the excited states, and is discussed further in Section VII.

There are three other possible combinations of three degenerate ground state irreps in which ΔT1−=ΔT1+=0\Delta_{T_{1-}}=\Delta_{T_{1+}}=0 along with one other irrep. According to Eq. 43 this is only possible when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0. Two such cases are possible, when ΔE=0\Delta_{E}=0 or ΔT2=0\Delta_{T_{2}}=0, corresponding to isolated triple points in the phase diagram. The third case with ΔA2=0\Delta_{A_{2}}=0 has no solutions. This exhausts all possibilities for three irreps to be degenerate in the ground state.

IV.3 The Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 Plane

Since the model space is a 3-sphere, the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 locus may be thought of as the “equator”, with the topology of a 2-sphere. It divides the 3-sphere into northern and southern hemispheres which are dual to each other under changing the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} and performing a π\pi spin rotation about the local axes. Within the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane this spin-rotation duality is promoted to a symmetry. Furthermore, within this subspace there is an additional duality: performing a π/2\pi/2 rotation of each spin about the local 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} sends Si±→∓i​Si±\cramped{S_{i}^{\pm}\to\mp iS_{i}^{\pm}}, which can be compensated by switching the sign of J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} Rau and Gingras 2019. Unlike the duality switching the sign of Jz±J_{z\pm} discussed in Section III.1, which relates two parameter sets in the same phase, reversing the sign of J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} relates different phases since it changes the irrep energies in Table 2. Referring to the ground states in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4, the J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm} duality switches ψ2↔ψ3\psi_{2}\leftrightarrow\psi_{3} and T2↔T1,planarT_{2}\leftrightarrow T_{1,\text{planar}}. This duality ensures that the phase boundaries will be symmetric across J±⁣±=0J_{\pm\pm}=0 within the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 subspace, and it is promoted to a symmetry when J±⁣±=Jz±=0J_{\pm\pm}=J_{z\pm}=0.

Within the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 subspace, the relevant couplings are Jz​zJ_{zz}, J±J_{\pm}, and J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm}, meaning that there is no direct coupling between the local easy-axis and easy-plane spin components. The ground states are therefore either easy-axis Ising orders (ferro- or antiferromagnetic), or easy-plane XY orders. The Ising ferromagnetic order occurs for dominant Jz​z≪0\cramped{J_{zz}\ll 0} and corresponds to the A2A_{2} all-in-all-out order. The Ising anti-ferromagnetic state occurs in the opposite limit Jz​z≫0\cramped{J_{zz}\gg 0}, corresponding to the T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} ground states. For dominant J±≫0\cramped{J_{\pm}\gg 0} the EE irrep is the ground state. Further selection of the energetically degenerate ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} configurations occurs due to order-by-disorder induced by asymmetric fluctuations about the ground state, discussed further in Section VI. Lastly, large J±⁣±≫0\cramped{J_{\pm\pm}\gg 0} selects the T2T_{2} order, while large J±⁣±≪0\cramped{J_{\pm\pm}\ll 0} selects the T1,planarT_{1,\text{planar}} configurations. Since Jz​z=0J_{zz}=0 is a degenerate case where the Hamiltonian becomes a pure XY model, it is standard to use Jz​zJ_{zz} as the energy scale, considering two separate cases depending on the sign of Jz​zJ_{zz}, while varying the ratios J±/|Jz​z|\cramped{J_{\pm}/|J_{zz}|} and J±⁣±/|Jz​z|\cramped{J_{\pm\pm}/|J_{zz}|}. This yields the two phase diagrams in Fig. 6(a) and (b).

IV.3.1 Line of T1T_{1} Degeneracy

Within these two diagrams one can clearly distinguish six triple points where three phases are degenerate, corresponding to the four lines and two special points that we identified in Table 3. The two special points occur when both T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate, at the ends of the line separating the T1,planarT_{1,\text{planar}} and T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} regions of the phase diagram. As we saw from Eq. 43, the degeneracy of the two T1T_{1} irreps is only possible when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, and meaning that there is no phase boundary between two distinct T1T_{1} phases when Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0, i.e. there is only a single T1T_{1} phase. It is therefore interesting to identify the locus on which the two T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate, i.e. all canting angles in Fig. 4 are degenerate, which is contained within the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 subspace. From Table 2 (setting JSIA=0J_{\text{SIA}}=0) this occurs when the square root which splits to the two T1T_{1} energies is zero, i.e. when

2​J±+4​J±⁣±+Jz​z=0andJz±=0.2J_{\pm}+4J_{\pm\pm}+J_{zz}=0\quad\text{and}\quad J_{z\pm}=0. (59)

The solutions of this equation can be parameterized by a single angle ϑ\vartheta as

(Jz​zJ±⁣±Jz±J±)=𝒩⁡(ϑ)​(2​cos⁡(ϑ)−4​sin⁡(ϑ)5​sin⁡(ϑ)0−cos⁡(ϑ)−8​sin⁡(ϑ))\begin{pmatrix}J_{zz}\\ J_{\pm\pm}\\ J_{z\pm}\\ J_{\pm}\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{N}(\vartheta)\begin{pmatrix}2\cos(\vartheta)-4\sin(\vartheta)\\ 5\sin(\vartheta)\\ 0\\ -\cos(\vartheta)-8\sin(\vartheta)\end{pmatrix} (60)

where 𝒩⁡(ϑ)>0\mathcal{N}(\vartheta)>0 is an arbitrary overall rescaling of the energy. These solutions are shown by the blue line in Fig. 6(a,b). Along this line all canted T1T_{1} configurations in Fig. 4 are degenerate. Indeed, part of this line forms the boundary between the T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} (pink) and T1,planarT_{1,\text{planar}} (red) portions of the phase diagram, clearly shown in Fig. 6(b).

IV.3.2 Stereographic Projection

In order to unify Fig. 6(a) and (b) into a single two-dimensional phase diagram, we consider the unit sphere in the space spanned by J±⁣±J_{\pm\pm}, Jz​zJ_{zz}, and J±J_{\pm}. This is the “equator” of the 3-sphere defined by Eq. 49. This 2-sphere is shown in Fig. 6(c), with the phases colored the same as in Fig. 6(a,b). In this figure the T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} region is on the back of the sphere and not visible. In order to visualize the entire surface of the sphere, we use the stereographic map defined by Eq. 55 to project the surface of the sphere onto a plane, as illustrated in Fig. 6(d). We have chosen the azimuthal axis to be the J±J_{\pm} axis, which becomes the radial direction on the projected surface. The top of the sphere is in the EE phase, so that after projecting onto a plane all of the phase boundaries appear near the origin, surrounded by the large-J±J_{\pm} EE phase, which extends to infinity.

IV.4 Big Picture: The Full Phase Diagram

We now have all the pieces to put together the full phase diagram using the stereographic projection Eq. 55 from the 3-sphere to 3-dimensional euclidean space. Using the projected Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane from Fig. 6 as our baseline, turning on Jz±J_{z\pm} takes us into the third (vertical) dimension. First, Footnote 13(a,b) adds to the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane the four triple lines, along each of which three irreps are degenerate and one is gapped. They are labeled and colored according to which irrep is gapped along that line with Footnote 13(a) showing an edge-one perspective and (b) showing a top-down view. All four meet at the two HAFM points above and below the plane, with the region above (below) this plane corresponding to Jz±J_{z\pm} positive (negative). The HAFM sits above the plane while its dual sits below the plane.

In order to visualize the phase boundaries in this three-dimensional space in a static two-dimensional image, it is convenient to deform the phase diagram in order to “straighten out” the four triple lines. We thus provide the topologically equivalent and simpler to visualize picture shown in Footnote 13(c). By choosing the “point at infinity” to be deep in the EE phase, all of the phase boundaries are located near the origin, and the exterior region is all in the EE phase. We could have chosen the point at infinity to be deep within any of the four phases, and obtained a qualitatively similar phase diagram with the other three phases located near the origin. We have colored the phase boundaries surrounding the A2A_{2} phase yellow, those surrounding the T2T_{2} phase blue, and those surrounding the T1T_{1} phase red. Gridlines on the phase boundaries are added as guides to the eye to emphasize the 3-dimensionality of the surfaces, but do not have any special meaning. We have excluded the Jz±>0J_{z\pm}>0 phase boundary between the T1T_{1} phase and the EE phase in order to show the interior region of the T1T_{1} phase and expose its phase boundaries with the A2A_{2} and T2T_{2} phases along with their triple line. Each of the four phases is enclosed by three phase boundaries where it touches one of the other phases. The Jz±≥0J_{z\pm}\geq 0 region of each phase is topologically equivalent to a tetrahedron, and the same for the Jz±≤0J_{z\pm}\leq 0 region, thus each phase has the topology of two tetrahedra glued along a triangular face. Footnote 13 constitutes a primary result of this work: a complete picture of the pyrochlore phase diagram showing all of the phases, phase boundaries, triple lines, and quadruple points.

V Topological Canting Cycles and Diabolical Locus

In this section we investigate the locus on which the two T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate, defined by Eq. 59. Whereas the energetic crossing of two different irreps in the ground state implies a phase transition, there is only one T1T_{1} phase in which the canting angle varies continuously, so the crossing of the T1T_{1} irreps is not a phase transition. This is a type of level repulsion: in order to make the square root zero in the last row of Table 2, we have to tune two separate parameter sets to be zero. Thus this locus is analogous to a conical intersection or diabolical point in the spectrum of a quantum system Berry and Wilkinson 1997, but in the space of parameters, known in quantum field theory as a diabolical locus Hsin et al. 2020. In Footnote 13 one can see that the locus where the two T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate (blue arc in the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane) “pierces” each of the T1⊕T2T_{1}\oplus T_{2} and T1⊕ET_{1}\oplus E phase boundaries once, giving rise to the two isolated triple points in the phase diagram. It passes within the T1T_{1} phase as a special line of degeneracy along which all canting angles are degenerate in the ground state, but it does not form a phase boundary. We have indicated with a small black loop a path surrounding the line of T1T_{1} degeneracy entirely contained within the T1T_{1} phase. Moving along such a loop, one T1T_{1} irrep is the unique ground state and the other is gapped, while the canting angle varies continuously. In other words the eigenvectors of the interaction matrix rotate in the T1T_{1} subspace, going around the cycle shown in Fig. 4. Starting from a point with T1−=T1,iceT_{1-}=T_{1,\text{ice}} (OPENθT1−=0)\theta_{T_{1-}}=0) and T1+=T1,planarT_{1+}=T_{1,\text{planar}}, going halfway around the loop the canting angle continuously rotates by π/4\pi/4 until the two T1T_{1} irreps have swapped, then continuing around the ground state returns to T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} but with all spins reversed, i.e. a π\pi rotation in Fig. 4. Going around the loop twice returns to the original ground state. Thus there is a topological winding number associated to paths in parameter space which enclose this locus, and we can identify it as a source of a sort of Berry curvature Berry and Wilkinson 1997.

V.1 Two Families of Hamiltonians

To investigate the canting behavior in more detail, as well as to illustrate the utility of having a complete phase diagram, we consider two particular one-parameter models—one which has constant canting angle and one on which the canting angle winds—and show how they fit in and are related in the phase diagram. Figure 8 shows the same phase diagram as Footnote 13(a,b), but with the “true” phase boundaries computed from the stereographic projection, rather than the deformed version shown in Footnote 13(c). Note in particular that the T1T_{1} phase appears larger than the A2A_{2} and T2T_{2} phases—while the T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} phases are symmetric in the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane, as seen in Footnote 13(b), turning on Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0 promotes the T1T_{1} phase (which is the ground state in the large-|Jz±||J_{z\pm}| limit).

The first family is what we will call the Heisenberg-plus-Jz±J_{z\pm} model, by tuning both JHeisJ_{\text{Heis}} from Eq. 2 and Jz±J_{z\pm} from Eq. 3. Up to an overall scale, this is a 1-parameter family of Hamiltonians, which can be parameterized as JHeis=cos⁡ϑJ_{\text{Heis}}=\cos\vartheta and Jz±=sin⁡ϑJ_{z\pm}=\sin\vartheta. This family is interesting because it corresponds to the triple line with A2A_{2}, EE and T2T_{2} degenerate, while both T1T_{1} irreps are tuned—the last triple line in Table 3 and the last column in Fig. 5. It is shown by the red circle in Fig. 8, which passes through both the Heisenberg ferromagnet (HFM) and anti-ferromagnet (HAFM) points, along with both of their duals. Part of this line lies on the triple intersection of the A2A_{2}, EE, and T2T_{2} phases, while the remainder passes through the T1T_{1} phase. Since this family encloses the line where both T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate, the canting angle winds by π\pi as we go around it while the two T1T_{1} irrep energies never cross, as seen in the last column of Fig. 5(c) and (d).

The second family is the Heisenberg-plus-Dzyloshinskii-Moriya (H+DM) line Elhajal et al. 2004; Elhajal et al. 2005; Canals et al. 2008; Noculak et al. 2023, with Hamiltonian
