In the future it will be interesting to study degenerate intersections of phases in more detail, and to determine whether any of them gives rise to a stable quantum spin liquid. Unfortunately in three dimensions there are few tools available to determine this. The only example where we have a meaningful level of analytical control is quantum spin ice, i.e. perturbing around the classical spin liquid point Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0 with all other couplings zero. There, we can perform a direct mapping from the spin Hamiltonian to a U(1) lattice gauge theory Hamiltonian Hermele et al. 2004, where the SizS_{i}^{z} operators map to electric field operators and the spin raising and lowering operators Si±S_{i}^{\pm} map to electric field raising and lowering operations exp⁡(±i​A),\exp(\pm iA), where AA is the lattice vector potential. This is only possible because the transverse fluctuations can be treated perturbatively on top of a classical Ising limit. This method—treating the classical ground state manifold as electric field eigenstates and spin-flipping terms as Wilson string operators—cannot be applied to study, say, the quantum HAFM, because the isotropic nature of the classical ground state means there is no preferred way to split spin operators into longitudinal and transverse components. Indeed the ground state of the quantum HAFM has been debated extensively, with the general view being that it exhibits some form of order, symmetry breaking, or dimensional reduction Canals and Garanin 2002; Iqbal et al. 2019; Hagymási et al. 2021; Astrakhantsev et al. 2021; Pohle et al. 2023; Schäfer et al. 2023. Similarly, the various tensor spin liquids arising from flat bands in the model discussed in this paper do not have a perturbative limit—all three spin components are used in the definition of the electric field, and all three also act as raising and lowering operators for each other—though there is some evidence that these quantum models do have some fractonic properties Han et al. 2022.

It will, in the long term, be interesting to determine whether the various degenerate loci in the pyrochlore phase diagram host quantum spin liquids. In particular, it will be interesting to understand the quantum ground states along the four triply degenerate lines and how they merge together at the quantum HAFM point. Previous studies have classified various types of quantum spin liquid mean field ground state wavefunctions compatible with the symmetries of the pyrochlore lattice Liu et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2021; Desrochers et al. 2022; Chern et al. 2022; Desrochers et al. 2023. Ref. Liu et al. 2019 emphasized how these are closely related to the competition of various intertwined irrep orders. Beyond mean field analysis, numerical methods are required. Unfortunately Quantum Monte Carlo algorithms are not generic enough to explore the entire phase diagram efficiently, and other powerful techniques like DMRG have extremely limited applicability in three dimensions. Relatively recently, pseudo-fermion functional renormalization (PFFRG) schemes have been developed which work well in three dimensions—see Ref. Müller et al. 2024 for a review—and applied to the pyrochlore lattice Iqbal et al. 2016; Iqbal et al. 2019; Niggemann et al. 2023; Noculak et al. 2023; Chern et al. 2024; Hagymási et al. 2024; Gresista et al. 2025. These methods can detect certain ordering instabilities and predict two-point correlation function, but involve uncontrolled approximations and so must be used in combinations with other numerical and analytical methods to approach the question of whether the quantum ground state avoids ordering and becomes a spin liquid.

VII Triple Degeneracies in Excited States

While we have discussed so far the cataloging of cases which have large degeneracies in the ground state and the resulting zero-energy flat bands, these high degeneracies can still be present even when they are not at zero energy. Such excited state degeneracies do not come into play in the ground state determination but may leave interesting imprints on the excitations above the ground state, e.g. in the spin wave (magnon) spectrum. As such, we close by briefly discussing the loci in the phase diagram where triple irrep collisions occur above zero energy. The effects of these enhanced degeneracies on the excitation spectrum within each phase will be an interesting topic for future study.

As mentioned previously, the triply-degenerate lines parameterized in Table 3 can be continued to negative ΔI′\Delta_{I^{\prime}} and form complete circles in the phase diagram, as is shown in Fig. 5. All four such lines wind non-trivially around the degenerate T1T_{1} locus. They are shown in Fig. 14(a) in the Jz±>0J_{z\pm}>0 half of the phase diagram, along with the two triple points. All four cycles intersect at the two fourfold-degenerate HAFM points. Each line, labeled by a single irrep I′I^{\prime} which is tuned while the others are kept degenerate, intersects the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane at two points, one where ΔI′>0\Delta_{I^{\prime}}>0 and one where ΔI′<0\Delta_{I^{\prime}}<0, which we have marked and labeled as (I′)0±(I^{\prime})^{0\pm} depending on the sign of ΔI′\Delta_{I^{\prime}}. The ΔE<0\Delta_{E}<0 line is not shown in its entirety as the stereographic projection maps the E0−E^{0-} point far from the origin. The (I′)0−(I^{\prime})^{0-} points are in a sense “centers” of their respective phases: they are the points where all three neighboring phases have equal and maximal gap, implying that these points are equidistant from all three phase boundaries. This can be seen in Fig. 5(c), where these points correspond to the left-most limit of each plot: the triply-degenerate irreps have JI=0J_{I}=0 at these points while ΔI′<0\Delta_{I^{\prime}}<0 reaches its minimum value. The line where both T1T_{1} irreps are tuned, corresponding to the Heisenberg-plus-Jz±J_{z\pm} model discussed in Section V.1, is slightly different. It cannot be parameterized by ΔT1−/ΔT1+\Delta_{T_{1-}}/\Delta_{T_{1+}} because both go negative on part of the path, so we have parameterized it instead by the splitting of the two T1T_{1} irreps. This line passes through two special points in the T1T_{1} phase, namely the Heisenberg ferromagnet and its dual. These may respectively be thought of as two different “centers” of the T1T_{1} phase, because in Fig. 8 one can see that the T1T_{1} phase appears to be the union of two roughly-spherical lobes centered on these two points.

These are not all of the triply degenerate cases, however, only the ones that are obtained from the four-fold degenerate HAFM by lifting the degeneracy of one irrep. The remaining ones are obtained by flipping the signs of all the couplings, i.e. changing the sign of the Hamiltonian H→−HH\to-H. This produces another set of triple lines which all intersect at the Heisenberg ferromagnet (HFM), shown in Fig. 14(b) along with two additional triple points, the pseudo-HFM and the ferromagnetic version of the DQQ (also appearing in Fig. 8). We have indicated the locations of the intersections of these lines with the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane, labeled the same as in Fig. 14(a) but with a minus sign to indicate these are the “ferro” counterparts. The I′=T1I^{\prime}=T_{1} line (red), corresponding to the Heisenberg-plus-Jz±J_{z\pm} model, is special because this family of Hamiltonians is mapped to itself under H→−HH\to-H. Since this line connects the HAFM and HFM points, it connects all of the triply-degenerate models together.

VIII Conclusion

In this paper we have considered in detail the structure of the classical phase diagram of rare-earth pyrochlore magnetic insulators with nearest-neighbor anisotropic interactions, described by the Hamiltonian Eqs. 2 and 3 with zero single-ion anisotropy.

In Section II we gave an intuitive derivation of the organization of spins into tensor order parameters, corresponding to the multipole moments of a single tetrahedron. We directly related the various tensor components to irreducible representations (irreps) of the tetrahedral symmetry group TdT_{d}, listed in Table 1, each of which corresponds to a ground state shown in Fig. 3. The presence of two copies of the T1T_{1} irrep results in the canting cycle shown in Fig. 4. We described how different irreps are coupled together, where the 3-components vector irreps serve as “fluxes” with corresponding “charges” given by the three components of A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E: raising the energy of a charge lowers the energy of its corresponding fluxes and vice-versa, and gapping a charge forces a zero-divergence condition on the corresponding flux.

In Section III we parameterized the model space—the space of equivalence classes of models differing by affine rescalings, topologically a 3-sphere—in terms of the relative irrep energies. This allowed us to perform an exhaustive search of all possible ground state degeneracies, which uncovered four triply-degenerate lines where three phases meet, listed in Table 3, all of which meet at the Heisenberg anti-ferromagnet point and its Jz±J_{z\pm}-dual, where all four phases become degenerate. Two isolated triple points also occur when Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0.

In Section IV we visualized the structure of the phase diagram by using a stereographic projection from the unit 3-sphere in the space of the four local couplings to ℝ3\mathbbm{R}^{3}. Since the phase diagram is reflection-symmetric about Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, we first mapped this stereographically in Fig. 6, which yields the phase diagram of non-Kramers pyrochlore magnets (for which Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0). We then mapped the phase diagram for Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0 (allowed for Kramers doublets) in Footnote 13, which exposes all of the phase boundaries, the four triply-degenerate lines, and shows how they merge at the two four-fold degenerate HAFM points. We also noted the locus along which the two T1T_{1} irreps are degenerate, which is a circle lying in the Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 plane. This locus pierces the T1⊕T2T_{1}\oplus T_{2} and T1⊕ET_{1}\oplus E phase boundaries, giving rise to the two isolated triple points in the phase diagram.

In Section V we discussed the T1T_{1}-degenerate locus in more detail. Going around any path in parameter space that links it the canting angle winds by π\pi. In Fig. 9 we showed how the phase diagram is foliated into 2-spheres on which the canting angle is constant, all of which intersection along the T1T_{1}-degenerate locus. This is analogous to “diabolical loci” which gives the phase diagram a topological structure not evident from energetic considerations alone. Adiabatically transporting the system around this locus within the T1T_{1} phase will cause the spins to perform a half-rotation around the canting cycle illustrated in Fig. 4. There is a topological invariant associated to 1-parameter families of Hamiltonians which identifies how many times they wind around the locus. We briefly described a general framework for such loci in frustrated magnets made of corner-sharing clusters in terms of homotopy groups of PSO(nn).

In Section VI we considered how the enhanced degeneracies obtained by collision of ground state irreps at classical multi-critical points can give rise to flat bands, and how these may lead to spin liquids. We provided a general discussion of the connection between flat bands and spin liquids, and discussed various ground state selection mechanisms that may co-opt the formation of a stable classical spin liquid. We provided an overview of known spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice obtained from the anisotropic Hamiltonian, and in Tables 6, 6 and 6 provided a catalog of all flat band degeneracies in the phase diagram, and identified which combinations of irreps yield flat band degeneracies which are more than the sum of their parts (i.e. intertwined) versus trivially stacked. In Figs. 10 and 11 we provided reference structure factors computed in the self-consistent Gaussian approximation for various interesting flat band cases, and described the relation between fourfold pinch points and pinch lines observed ubiquitously in these models: Fig. 13 demonstrates the 3D structure of the pinched correlations at the intersection of pinch lines, which when cut produce fourfold pinch points.

Lastly, in Section VII we identified all loci in the phase diagram where three irreps are degenerate above the ground state, including both the continuation of the triple phase degeneracies into each phase along with their ferro-counterparts which all intersect at the Heisenberg ferromagnetic points. This is summarized in Fig. 14.

Beyond the issue of whether any of the flat band cases we have cataloged host stable quantum spin liquids, in the future it will be of interest to extend the analysis here to study the broader phase diagram of breathing pyrochlores, which can have different couplings on the two symmetry-inequivalent sets of tetrahedra and may host additional spin liquids Essafi et al. 2017b; Ghosh et al. 2019; Chern et al. 2022. Furthermore, there may be surprising physics to be gleaned within the ordered phases of the pyrochlore in the spectrum of (magnon) excitations, as evidenced by the extended T1T_{1}-degenerate locus and the various lines of high degeneracy in the band structure above zero energy. Lastly, it will be interesting to study in more detail the canting cycle in the pyrochlore and other frustrated magnets, to explore its potential connections to diabolical loci, symmetry pumps, and boundary symmetry breaking, and whether it has experimentally observable consequences.

Beyond the pyrochlore Hamiltonian considered here, the methods used in this paper are applicable to other models. For example, in Ref. Chung et al. 2025 we have applied the same methods to study the equivalent of Eq. 3 with spins (dipole operators) replaced by quadrupoles, which increases the number of degrees of freedom, and for which one can similarly identify diabolical loci and spin liquids arising from the collision of irreps. In general, flat band classical spin liquids arise in Hamiltonians which enforce local constraints, sometimes called “constrainer Hamiltonians” Yan et al. 2024a; Yan et al. 2024b; Benton and Moessner 2021; Henley 2010. In the pyrochlore model considered here, the local constraint is that ground states have zero overlap with the gapped irreps on each tetrahedron. In general constrainer Hamiltonians, the local constraints involve a constellation of dipole operators—spins—and it is natural that different constraints correspond to extinction of certain multipole moments of the spin distribution, and correspondingly to the collision of ground state irreps. It will be interesting to extend this to further-neighbor interactions and other lattices, and to eventually perform a complete symmetry classification of constrainer Hamiltonians.

Appendix A Coordinate Conventions

Although not crucial for the results presented in this paper, for completeness we provide a set of coordinates for the local bases and parameterizations discussed throughout the paper. Defining the cubic axes of the pyrochlore crystal structure to be along the three Cartesian axes 𝒆^x,𝒆^y,𝒆^z\hat{\bm{e}}_{x},\hat{\bm{e}}_{y},\hat{\bm{e}}_{z}, the FCC primitive vectors can be given by

𝒂1=a0​𝒆^x+𝒆^y2,𝒂2=a0​𝒆^y+𝒆^z2,𝒂3=a0​𝒆^z+𝒆^x2,\bm{a}_{1}=a_{0}\frac{\hat{\bm{e}}_{x}+\hat{\bm{e}}_{y}}{2},\quad\bm{a}_{2}=a_{0}\frac{\hat{\bm{e}}_{y}+\hat{\bm{e}}_{z}}{2},\quad\bm{a}_{3}=a_{0}\frac{\hat{\bm{e}}_{z}+\hat{\bm{e}}_{x}}{2}, (91)

where a0a_{0} is the cubic conventional cell lattice constant. The four FCC sublattice vectors, corresponding to the four corners of a tetrahedron, can then be given by

𝒄1=𝟎,𝒄2=𝒂1/2,𝒄3=𝒂2/2,𝒄4=𝒂3/2.\bm{c}_{1}=\bm{0},\quad\bm{c}_{2}=\bm{a}_{1}/2,\quad\bm{c}_{3}=\bm{a}_{2}/2,\quad\bm{c}_{4}=\bm{a}_{3}/2. (92)

The centers of the tetrahedra form a bipartite diamond lattice with sublattice positions

𝜹±=±14∑μ=14𝒄μ,\bm{\delta}_{\pm}=\pm\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\mu=1}^{4}\bm{c}_{\mu}, (93)

where we use μ\mu to index the FCC sublattices of the pyrochlore lattice. The four sublattice easy-axis vectors can be then be specified by normalizing the displacement vector from the center of a tetrahedron to each corner,

𝒛^μ=𝒄μ−𝜹+|𝒄μ−𝜹+|.\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}=\frac{\bm{c}_{\mu}-\bm{\delta}_{+}}{|\bm{c}_{\mu}-\bm{\delta}_{+}|}. (94)

Using the notation

[a​b​c]≡a​𝒆^x+b​𝒆^y+c​𝒆^z[abc]\equiv a\hat{\bm{e}}_{x}+b\hat{\bm{e}}_{y}+c\hat{\bm{e}}_{z} (95)

along with a¯≡−a\bar{a}\equiv-a, we can provide bases for the local frames at each corner of the tetrahedron (up to normalization),

𝒙^1\displaystyle\hat{\bm{x}}_{1} ∝[11​2¯]𝒙^2∝[1¯​1¯​2¯]𝒙^3∝[1¯​12]𝒙^4∝[1​1¯​2]\displaystyle\propto[11\bar{2}]\quad\hat{\bm{x}}_{2}\propto[\bar{1}\bar{1}\bar{2}]\quad\hat{\bm{x}}_{3}\propto[\bar{1}12]\quad\hat{\bm{x}}_{4}\propto[1\bar{1}2]
𝒚^1\displaystyle\hat{\bm{y}}_{1} ∝[1​1¯​0]𝒚^2∝[1¯​10]𝒚^3∝[1¯​1¯​0]𝒚^4∝[110]\displaystyle\propto[1\bar{1}0]\quad\hat{\bm{y}}_{2}\propto[\bar{1}10]\quad\hat{\bm{y}}_{3}\propto[\bar{1}\bar{1}0]\quad\hat{\bm{y}}_{4}\propto[110]
𝒛^1\displaystyle\hat{\bm{z}}_{1} ∝[1¯​1¯​1¯]𝒛^2∝[11​1¯]𝒛^3∝[1​1¯​1]𝒛^4∝[1¯​11].\displaystyle\propto[\bar{1}\bar{1}\bar{1}]\quad\hat{\bm{z}}_{2}\propto[11\bar{1}]\quad\hat{\bm{z}}_{3}\propto[1\bar{1}1]\quad\hat{\bm{z}}_{4}\propto[\bar{1}11]. (96)

These are shown in Fig. 15. The 𝒙^μ\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mu} vectors have been chosen to lie in mirror planes, while the 𝒚^μ\hat{\bm{y}}_{\mu} vectors lie along a C2C_{2} rotation axis. With these convention, referring to Fig. 3 and Fig. 4, ψ2\psi_{2} has all spins along 𝒙^μ\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mu}; ψ3\psi_{3} has all spins along 𝒚^μ\hat{\bm{y}}_{\mu}, T2T_{2} has two spins along 𝒚^μ\hat{\bm{y}}_{\mu} and two along −𝒚^μ-\hat{\bm{y}}_{\mu}; T1,planarT_{1,\text{planar}} has two spins along 𝒙^μ\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mu} and two along −𝒙^μ-\hat{\bm{x}}_{\mu}; A2A_{2} has all spins along 𝒛^μ\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}; and T1,iceT_{1,\text{ice}} has two spins along 𝒛^μ\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu} and two along −𝒛^μ-\hat{\bm{z}}_{\mu}.

Appendix B Fourier Transforms

Due to translation invariance the interaction matrix in Eq. 1a is diagonal in the Fourier basis. We take the system to consist of L3L^{3} unit cells with periodic boundaries, in which case

𝒥μ​να​β​(𝒒,𝒒′)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q},\bm{q}^{\prime}) ≡1L3∑i∈μ∑j∈νJi​jα​βei​𝒒⋅𝒓je−i𝒒′⋅𝒓i\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{L^{3}}\sum_{i\in\mu}\sum_{j\in\nu}J_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{j}}e^{-i\bm{q}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{r}_{i}}
=δ𝒒,𝒒′∑j∈νJi​jα​βei​𝒒⋅(𝒓j−𝒓j)(i∈μ)\displaystyle=\delta_{\bm{q},\bm{q}^{\prime}}\sum_{j\in\nu}J_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{j}-\bm{r}_{j})}\quad(i\in\mu)
≡δ𝒒,𝒒′​Jμ​να​β​(𝒒),\displaystyle\equiv\delta_{\bm{q},\bm{q}^{\prime}}J_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q}), (97)

where the sums are restricted to sites in a single sublattice. For nearest-neighbor interactions it is useful to define a modified adjacency matrix of the pyrochlore lattice,

𝒜i​j={1i,j are nearest-neighbors,1/2i=j,0otherwise,\mathcal{A}_{ij}=\begin{cases}1&\quad\text{$i,j$ are nearest-neighbors,}\\ 1/2&\quad i=j,\\ 0&\quad\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (98)

whose Fourier transform is

𝒜μ​ν​(𝒒)=(2−δμ​ν)​cos⁡[𝒒⋅(𝒄μ−𝒄ν)].\mathcal{A}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q})=(2-\delta_{\mu\nu})\cos[\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{c}_{\mu}-\bm{c}_{\nu})]. (99)

The Fourier transformed nearest-neighbor interaction matrix is then

𝒥μ​να​β​(𝒒)=Jμ​να​β​𝒜μ​ν​(𝒒),\mathcal{J}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q})=J_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}\,\mathcal{A}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q}), (100)

where the 12×1212\times 12 matrix Jμ​να​βJ_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta} is given in Eq. 103. The on-site term in Eq. 98 is added to allow for the on-site single-ion anisotropy interaction, which is double counted in the unrestricted double sum in Eq. 1a. For reciprocal space we use Miller indices relative to the cubic conventional unit cell, denoted with round brackets

𝒒=2​πa0​(h​𝒆^x+k​𝒆^y+l​𝒆^z)≡(h​k​l).\bm{q}=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}}(h\hat{\bm{e}}_{x}+k\hat{\bm{e}}_{y}+l\hat{\bm{e}}_{z})\equiv(hkl). (101)

Figure 16 shows the first Brillouin zone of the FCC lattice with high-symmetry points, lines, and planes marked.

Appendix C Mapping Between Parameterizations

The number of free parameters in the interaction matrix 𝒥\mathcal{J} in Eq. 1a is restricted by symmetry. A given space group GG acts on the spin configuration SiαS_{i}^{\alpha} by permutation of the site index ii and pseudovector rotation of the spin components index α\alpha. For nearest-neighbor interactions in the (non-breathing) pyrochlore lattice, the interaction matrix is the same on every tetrahedron, so the symmetry constraints can be obtained from just looking at the symmetry group of the tetrahedron, TdT_{d}, with action defined by the representation ρ\rho in Eq. 9. The allowed spin-spin couplings can be deduced from the fact that the Hamiltonian on a tetrahedron reduces to a sum over the irrep order parameters squared, or more generally by solving the equations

[𝒥,ρ⁡(g)]=0∀g∈Gand𝒥=𝒥T.[\mathcal{J},\rho(g)]=0\quad\forall g\in G\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{J}^{\mathrm{T}}. (102)

C.2 Global Frame Coordinate-Free

In Eq. 2 we provided another version of the Hamiltonian with various named interactions: Heisenberg, pseudo-dipolar, Kitaev-like, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM). Their definitions are provided by Fig. 1. They are directly related to the global-basis parameters J1J_{1} through J4J_{4}. It suffices to compare the interaction matrix Jμ​να​βJ_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta} in Eq. 103 for a single pair μ≠ν\mu\neq\nu. With the conventions for the vectors given in Fig. 1 and Appendix A, we have the identification for sublattices μ=1\mu=1 and ν=2\nu=2

(J1J3−J4J3J1−J4J4J4J2)=(JHeis+JPD/2JPD/2JDM/2JPD/2JHeis+JPD/2JDM/2−JDM/2−JDM/2JHeis+JK).\begin{pmatrix}[c]J_{1}&J_{3}&-J_{4}\\ J_{3}&J_{1}&-J_{4}\\ J_{4}&J_{4}&J_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}[c]J_{\text{Heis}}+J_{\text{PD}}/2&J_{\text{PD}}/2&J_{\text{DM}}/\sqrt{2}\\ J_{\text{PD}}/2&J_{\text{Heis}}+J_{\text{PD}}/2&J_{\text{DM}}/\sqrt{2}\\ -J_{\text{DM}}/\sqrt{2}&-J_{\text{DM}}/\sqrt{2}&J_{\text{Heis}}+J_{\text{K}}\end{pmatrix}. (104)

C.3 Local Frame

To obtain the local basis Eq. 3, let RμR_{\mu} denote the SO(3) matrices rotating from the global Cartesian basis {𝒆^x,𝒆^y,𝒆^z}\{\hat{\bm{e}}_{x},\hat{\bm{e}}_{y},\hat{\bm{e}}_{z}\} to the local basis on each sublattice defined by Eq. 94 and Eq. 96, and let QQ denote the non-unitary transformation

Q=(1i01−i0001):(Sμx,Sμy,Sμz)↦(Sμ+,Sμ−,Sμz),Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&i&0\\ 1&-i&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}:(S^{x}_{\mu},S^{y}_{\mu},S^{z}_{\mu})\mapsto(S^{+}_{\mu},S^{-}_{\mu},S^{z}_{\mu}), (105)

let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the block-diagonal matrix diag⁡(R1,R2,R3,R4)\diag(R_{1},R_{2},R_{3},R_{4}) and let 𝒬\mathscr{Q} denote the block-diagonal matrix diag⁡(Q,Q,Q,Q)\diag(Q,Q,Q,Q). Then the local couplings in Eq. 3 are obtained by transforming Eq. 103 as3232 32 Note that we are taking the Hamiltonian to be defined by the complex sesquilinear inner product, H=𝑺†⋅𝒥⋅𝑺/2H=\bm{S}^{\dagger}\cdot\mathcal{J}\cdot\bm{S}/2. Because of this, the Si+​Sj−S^{+}_{i}S^{-}_{j} terms appears as diagonal components in 𝒥local\mathcal{J}_{\text{local}}, while the Si+​Sj+S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{+} terms appear as off-diagonal components. Note further that 𝒥local\mathcal{J}_{\text{local}} and 𝒥global\mathcal{J}_{\text{global}} do not have the same eigenvalues as 𝒬\mathscr{Q} is not unitary.

𝒥local=(𝒬−1)†​ℛ​𝒥global​ℛ−1​𝒬−1,\mathcal{J}_{\text{local}}=(\mathscr{Q}^{-1})^{\dagger}\mathcal{R}\,\mathcal{J}_{\text{global}}\,\mathcal{R}^{-1}\mathscr{Q}^{-1}, (106)

Appendix D SCGA Structure Factors

In the self-consistent Gaussian approximation (SCGA), the spin length constraint is relaxed to a Gaussian distribution whose variance is enforced by a Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda. Given a quadratic spin Hamiltonian HH of the form Eq. 1a, we define the SCGA Hamiltonian

HSCGA=H+T​∑iλi​|𝑺i|2,H_{\text{SCGA}}=H+T\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}|\bm{S}_{i}|^{2}, (108)

where TT is temperature. The partition function is then simply a multivariate Gaussian integral,

ZSCGA=∫∏i,αdSiαexp(−∑i​j∑α​βSiα(λi​δi​j​δα​β⏟Λi​jα​β+β𝒥i​jα​β)Sjβ),Z_{\text{SCGA}}=\int\prod_{i,\alpha}\mathrm{d}S_{i}^{\alpha}\,\exp(-\sum_{ij}\sum_{\alpha\beta}S_{i}^{\alpha}(\underbrace{\lambda_{i}\delta_{ij}\delta_{\alpha\beta}}_{\Lambda_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}}+\beta\mathcal{J}_{ij}^{\alpha\beta})S_{j}^{\beta}), (109)

where β=1/T\beta=1/T is the inverse temperature and δ\delta is the Kronecker delta. Correlation functions are then simply given by

⟨Siα​Sjβ⟩≡𝒢i​jα​β=([Λ+β​𝒥]−1)i​jα​β.\langle S_{i}^{\alpha}S_{j}^{\beta}\rangle\equiv\mathcal{G}_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}=([\Lambda+\beta\mathcal{J}]^{-1})_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}. (110)

The Lagrange multipliers are solved for self-consistently via the constraint

1=⟨|𝑺i|2⟩=∑α([Λ+β​𝒥]−1)i​iα​α.1=\langle|\bm{S}_{i}|^{2}\rangle=\sum_{\alpha}([\Lambda+\beta\mathcal{J}]^{-1})_{ii}^{\alpha\alpha}. (111)

Since every site is symmetry-equivalent in the pyrochlore lattice, the Lagrange multipliers are all the same, λi≡λ\lambda_{i}\equiv\lambda, and the self-consistency condition can be solved by averaging over all sites,

1=1Nspins​Tr⁡[λ​𝟙+β​𝒥]−1,1=\frac{1}{N_{\text{spins}}}\Tr[\lambda\mathbbm{1}+\beta\mathcal{J}]^{-1}, (112)

where 𝟙\mathbbm{1} is the 12​L312L^{3}-dimensional identity matrix. We assume that the minimum eigenvalue of 𝒥\mathcal{J} has been shifted to zero, let ℱ\mathscr{F} denote the kernel of 𝒥\mathcal{J}, and let N0=dimℱN_{0}=\dim\mathscr{F} denote the number of zero eigenvalues of 𝒥\mathcal{J} (if not, then let vv denote the minimum eigenvalue and redefine 𝒥→𝒥−v​𝟙\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{J}-v\mathbbm{1} and Λ→Λ+β​v​𝟙\Lambda\to\Lambda+\beta v\mathbbm{1}). In the limit of high temperature β→0\beta\to 0 the solution is λ=3\lambda=3 (the number of spin components). In the low-temperature limit β→∞\beta\to\infty all positive eigenvalues of 𝒥\mathcal{J} are suppressed in the inverse, and the solution is λ=N0/Nspins\lambda=N_{0}/N_{\text{spins}}. If N0N_{0} is subextensive then N0/Nspins→0N_{0}/N_{\text{spins}}\to 0 in the thermodynamic limit Nspins→∞N_{\text{spins}}\to\infty, meaning that λ\lambda vanishes at some critical temperature TcT_{c}, indicating a phase transition as the stiffness of the zero-energy modes vanishes, and a breakdown of the SCGA below TcT_{c}. If the number of zero eigenvalues is extensive, i.e. 𝒥\mathcal{J} has zero-energy flat bands, with N0=3​Nspins​fN_{0}=3N_{\text{spins}}f for 0<f=nflat/ntot<10<f=n_{\text{flat}}/n_{\text{tot}}<1, then the solution is λ=3​f\lambda=3f. The zero-temperature correlation functions are then given by the projector PℱP_{\mathscr{F}} to the kernel of 𝒥\mathcal{J},

limT→0𝒢=13​f​Pℱ.\lim_{T\to 0}\mathcal{G}=\frac{1}{3f}P_{\mathscr{F}}. (113)

We use this formula to calculate the structure factor plots in Figs. 10 and 11.
